articles.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
articles.text:
If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.
The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
The new promo drops Apple’s 13-incher to within $100 of its all-time low, easing the sting of recent price hikes.
The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount, is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.
Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model, the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display, or one of the M6-powered machines. A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

articles.title: iPhone Duo: Apple bringt Gesichtserkennung per Software-Update
articles.text:
iPhone Duo: Apple bringt Gesichtserkennung per Software-Update
Mit einem Startpreis von 2.300 Euro ist das iPhone Duo Apples mit Abstand teuerstes Smartphone. Trotzdem bekommt man nicht in jedem Bereich die besten Komponenten. Im Vergleich zu den Pro-Modellen muss man Abstriche bei der Kamera machen, mit Blick auf alle anderen iPhones zudem bei der Entsperrmethode. Während selbst das günstige iPhone 17e mit der Gesichtserkennung Face-ID ausgestattet ist, muss man sich am teuren Duo per Fingerabdruck authentifizieren.
Laut Apple hat das den Vorteil, dass man das iPhone unabhängig davon, ob es geöffnet oder geschlossen ist, auf dieselbe Weise entsperren kann. Eine Erklärung, warum das Unternehmen auf die Face-ID-Technik verzichtet hat, gibt es nicht. Möglicherweise sind Platzprobleme im kompakten Gehäuse die Ursache. Trotzdem will Apple das iPhone Duo mit iOS 27.3 nun um eine Gesichtserkennung erweitern, wie unter anderem Wired berichtet.
iPhone Duo bekommt Gesichtserkennung ohne Face ID
Zu finden ist die neue Funktion zunächst in der zweiten Entwickler-Beta von iOS 27.3 in den Einstellungen für „Touch ID & Code“. Laut 9t05Mac ist der Einrichtungsprozess ähnlich gestaltet wie jener von Face-ID. Nutzer:innen müssen dafür lediglich einmal kurz nach rechts, links, oben und unten schauen. Wired zufolge bedient sich Apple hier der Technologie, die auch im Smarthome-Display Homeview zum Einsatz kommt, um bis zu sechs Nutzer:innen zu identifizieren. Dabei werden allerdings auch weitere Faktoren wie die Stimmen berücksichtigt. Das System sei allerdings nicht so umfassend wie Face-ID und könnte anfälliger für Angriffe sein.
Wohl auch deswegen beschränkt Apple, was man mit der neuen Entsperrmethode machen kann. Während ihr Face-ID unter anderem nutzen könnt, um Zahlungen via Apple Pay zu autorisieren („Pay with your Face“) oder die Passwort-App freizuschalten, könnt ihr mit der Gesichtserkennung auf dem Duo lediglich das iPhone entsperren. Für alles Weitere ist nach wie vor der Fingerabdruck oder aber die Eingabe des Display-Codes nötig. Außerdem müsst ihr die Funktion alle 45 Minuten erneut per Fingerabdruck oder Code-Eingabe aktivieren. Und: Mit der „Facetime“-Kamera des inneren Displays funktioniert die Lösung nicht. Das Entsperren per Gesichtserkennung ist im aufgefalteten Modus also nicht möglich.
iPhone Duo sperrt sich beim Schließen
Neben der neuen Entsperrmethode kommt das praktische Gegenteil hinzu: Das Duo lässt sich so einstellen, dass es sich sperrt, wenn man es zuklappt. Bislang wird durch den Vorgang der äußere Bildschirm aktiviert. Nutzer:innen müssen proaktiv auf die Seitentaste drücken, um das iPhone zu sperren.
Wann genau das Update auf iOS 27.3 erscheint, ist bislang nicht bekannt. Apple hatte aber den Start der neuen Health-App für Ende 2026 versprochen. Sie ist (bislang) Teil von iOS 27.3.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Omata AI turns WhatsApp into a business operating system for SMEs
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Omata AI has built a WhatsApp-native business operating system that helps small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) manage their day-to-day operations through simple conversations.
The flagship product of Autonomous Data Enterprise, a company founded in 2026 by Stanley Okafor, Omata AI lets merchants record sales, manage inventory, track customer balances and monitor business performance by sending WhatsApp messages. A connected dashboard gives them more oversight.
“Our vision is to make business management as easy as sending a WhatsApp message,” Okafor told Disrupt Africa. “For example, a trader can send a message such as, “I sold two bags of rice for NGN50,000”, and Omata AI can interpret the information, prepare a structured transaction and request the merchant’s approval before confirmation.”
Okafor said that many small businesses across Africa still rely on notebooks, memory and scattered WhatsApp chats to manage their records. Existing accounting, POS and inventory tools are often too complex or too costly for them.
“Rather than asking merchants to adapt to complicated software, we want business software to adapt to the way they already operate,” he said.
The startup’s main differentiator is what Okafor calls a “human-approval-first” architecture. Under this design, AI cannot change financial records without the business owner’s sign-off.
“Unlike a general-purpose chatbot, a business-management system cannot afford to misinterpret figures or process the same transaction repeatedly,” he said.
Omata AI is founder-funded and pre-revenue. It is currently working with 10 merchants in early-stage pilots, and it is entered in the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon 2026. The startup plans to adopt a subscription model with affordable entry-level plans for individual traders.
“We are prioritising product validation, merchant feedback and operational reliability rather than aggressively scaling user numbers,” Okafor said.
The startup is focused on Nigeria for now but plans a gradual expansion into other African markets where WhatsApp is widely used for business.

Normalmente, te diríamos que las mejores ofertas no suelen durar hasta los últimos días de noviembre, pero de vez en cuando encontramos algún chollo flash el último viernes del mes. Y en esta ocasión, dicho chollo está protagonizado por el Pixel 11: ha caído hasta los 685 euros en su versión de 512 GB.
Google Pixel 11 - Smartphone Android libre - Glaciar, 512GB | Con Gemini Intelligence, batería de más de 30 horas y pantalla Super Actua de 6,3"

Aunque eso sí: solo en un color y, según indica Amazon en la página del móvil, parecen no quedar demasiadas unidades.
Estamos ante un móvil compacto que apenas pesa 195 gramos y que tiene 7,6 milímetros de grosor. articles.title: La reflexión de Albert Einstein sobre las personas independientes: "La monotonía y la soledad de una vida tranquila estimulan la mente creativa"
articles.text:
Albert Einstein tenía una propuesta bastante peculiar para los jóvenes que querían dedicarse a la ciencia: trabajar en un faro. No lo decía de broma. En octubre de 1933, durante una intervención en Londres, el físico defendió que algunos empleos tranquilos podían ser una buena alternativa para quienes necesitaban tiempo libre para investigar. Su preocupación era que muchos científicos estuvieran demasiado ocupados intentando ganarse la vida.
En aquella conferencia también habló de su propia experiencia viviendo apartado en el campo. Fue entonces cuando explicó que había comprobado cómo "la monotonía de una vida tranquila estimula la mente creativa". La frase, recuperada por OKDIARIO en un artículo sobre las personas independientes, resumía algo que Einstein valoraba especialmente: poder dedicar horas a pensar sin demasiadas interrupciones.
Por qué Einstein prefería un faro a una beca de investigación
El científico consideraba que trabajar en un faro podía dejar tiempo suficiente para estudiar matemáticas o filosofía. La idea tenía su lógica: en lugar de depender de una beca de investigación, un joven podría tener un empleo con el que mantenerse y reservar parte del día para desarrollar sus propios proyectos.
Einstein también cuestionó las dificultades que encontraban quienes recibían ayudas para investigar. A su juicio, la obligación de presentar resultados en periodos demasiado cortos podía perjudicar trabajos que necesitaban años de dedicación. Por eso pensaba que disponer de tranquilidad y cierta independencia económica podía ser más útil de lo que parecía.
Aquella propuesta no llegó a convertirse en un sistema de empleo para investigadores, pero tampoco fue una ocurrencia aislada. Einstein ya había defendido anteriormente la posibilidad de combinar un trabajo remunerado con la investigación científica. En su intervención de 1933 volvió a plantear esa alternativa, esta vez con un oficio muy concreto: cuidar de un faro.

articles.title: pCloud Pass a bien été victime d'une cyberattaque, l'éditeur assure que vos mots de passe sont en sécurité
articles.text:
Quelques heures après les premiers signalements de connexions suspectes à pCloud Pass, l'entreprise suisse confirme avoir subi une cyberattaque. Si des adresses mail ont été exposées, l'éditeur assure que les données conservées dans les coffres-forts de son gestionnaire de mots de passe n'ont pas été compromises.
Nous vous en parlions ce vendredi matin. Dans la nuit du 26 au 27 novembre, plusieurs utilisateurs et utilisatrices de pCloud Pass ont reçu des notifications leur signalant la connexion d'un appareil inconnu à leur compte, malgré l'activation de la double authentification. Nous avions nous-mêmes reçu cette alerte et relevé plusieurs anomalies dans les infrastructures de pCloud. L'entreprise a depuis pris la parole sur Reddit pour apporter de premiers éléments d'explication.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Des adresses mail exposées, mais des coffres-forts épargnés selon pCloud
L'entreprise suisse indique avoir rapidement contenu une cyberattaque visant son gestionnaire de mots de passe. L'attaque a toutefois entraîné l'exposition des adresses mail d'un nombre limité d'utilisateurs et utilisatrices de pCloud Pass, sans que l'éditeur précise combien de personnes sont concernées. D'après pCloud, les notifications reçues cette nuit auraient été déclenchées par des tentatives de connexion à leurs comptes.
L'entreprise assure en revanche que les mots de passe, les notes et les autres informations enregistrées dans les coffres-forts de ses clients n'ont pas été compromis. Elle rappelle que ces données sont chiffrées sur les appareils de ces derniers et que leur déchiffrement nécessite de connaître leur mot de passe maître, auquel l'éditeur lui-même n'a pas accès.
L'attaque aurait par ailleurs été circonscrite à pCloud Pass, épargnant les services de stockage en ligne de l'entreprise. Compte tenu de l'exposition des adresses mail, pCloud invite néanmoins ses clients à redoubler de vigilance face aux tentatives de phishing et rappelle qu'elle ne leur demandera jamais de communiquer leur mot de passe maître ou leurs mots de récupération.
Les explications de pCloud laissent les internautes perplexes
Sur Reddit comme à la rédaction, les explications de pCloud peinent à convaincre. Les notifications reçues cette nuit ne nous informaient pas d'une tentative de connexion à notre compte, mais bien de la connexion d'un nouvel appareil. Plusieurs internautes ont même indiqué avoir retrouvé cet appareil dans la liste de leurs sessions actives, malgré l'activation de la double authentification. On ignore aussi pourquoi les adresses IP associées à ces connexions appartenaient aux propres infrastructures de pCloud et pourquoi les liens intégrés aux notifications renvoyaient vers ce qui semble être un environnement de test interne à l'entreprise.
À défaut de savoir à quelles ressources les pirates ont pu accéder, il est également difficile d'évaluer la portée de l'attaque sur les coffres-forts. Si pCloud assure que leur contenu n'a pas été compromis, l'entreprise ne précise pas si les attaquants ont pu en récupérer des copies chiffrées. Or, comme nous l'expliquions hier à la suite de la cyberattaque dont a été victime 1Password, le chiffrement de bout en bout ne suffit pas toujours à garantir la sécurité des mots de passe lorsque les infrastructures du gestionnaire sont compromises.
Plus surprenant, pCloud consacre une partie de sa communication aux progrès de l'intelligence artificielle, qui accélèrent la découverte de vulnérabilités dans les logiciels, parfois avant même que leurs développeurs n'aient pu les identifier et les corriger. L'entreprise ne livre pourtant aucun détail sur la méthode employée par les pirates pour s'en prendre à pCloud Pass, ni sur le rôle éventuel de l'IA dans cette attaque.
Contactée à deux reprises par nos soins ce vendredi, l'entreprise n'a toujours pas répondu à nos questions.
Vous avez reçu une notification de pCloud Pass, que faire ?
Si vous avez reçu l'une de ces notifications, connectez-vous directement à pCloud Pass, sans passer par les liens intégrés au mail. Vérifiez la liste des appareils connectés et révoquez les sessions que vous ne reconnaissez pas. Par précaution, changez également le mot de passe de votre compte pCloud et celui de votre coffre-fort, et assurez-vous que la double authentification est toujours activée.
Attention, le renouvellement de votre mot de passe maître vise à sécuriser vos futurs accès au coffre-fort, mais ne protège pas une éventuelle copie de celui-ci déjà dérobée par les pirates. Redoublez enfin de vigilance face aux mails se réclamant de l'entreprise, les attaquants pouvant exploiter les adresses mail exposées pour mener des campagnes de phishing.

articles.title: Un trou de la couche d’ozone record et pourtant la situation n’est pas si grave : comment est-ce possible ?
articles.text:
27,3 millions de kilomètres carrés. C’est la taille atteinte le 20 septembre 2026 par le trou de la couche d’ozone au-dessus de l’Antarctique, soit près de deux fois la superficie du continent glacé et 31 % de plus que la moyenne des vingt dernières années à la même période. Ces chiffres, communiqués par l’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) le 26 novembre 2026, nous viennent du programme européen d’observation de la Terre Copernicus, et plus précisément de Sentinel-5P, un satellite chargé de surveiller l’état de l’atmosphère terrestre depuis 2017.
Ce trou est en réalité un appauvrissement de la couche d’ozone au-dessus de l’Antarctique, qui se forme chaque année au printemps austral, quand le froid extrême de la stratosphère polaire favorise la destruction de l’ozone. Le phénomène est saisonnier et dépend aussi du retour du soleil, mais il est d’abord provoqué par les activités humaines, et plus précisément par les CFC et autres gaz chlorés ou bromés longtemps utilisés dans les aérosols, les réfrigérateurs ou les climatiseurs. Voir l’un des plus grands trous en près d’un demi-siècle peut donc paraître inquiétant à première vue – pourtant, la situation n’est pas si simple, et surtout pas si catastrophique.
Un trou plus grand, mais pas plus profond
Pour commencer, la taille du trou varie énormément d’une année sur l’autre. Le trou de 2026 compte parmi les plus étendus jamais mesurés, alors que celui de 2025 était le cinquième plus petit depuis 1992 selon la NASA et la NOAA, avec un pic à 22,9 millions de kilomètres carrés le 9 septembre. Or, la quantité de CFC et d’autres gaz destructeurs d’ozone dans l’atmosphère baisse lentement et régulièrement depuis le début des années 2000. Elle ne peut pas expliquer un tel écart en un an, pas plus que les émissions de gaz à effet de serre.
L’ESA indique que si la superficie du trou est en effet très importante cette année, ce n’est pas le cas de sa profondeur. Il s’agit ici d’une autre donnée : le niveau d’appauvrissement de l’ozone. Celui-ci reste plutôt dans la moyenne de ces dernières années d’après les données de Sentinel-5P, ce qui indique que les efforts de ces dernières décennies pour préserver cette couche d’ozone sont bel et bien récompensés et que la perte d’ozone dans l’atmosphère n’est plus aussi élevée qu’elle ne l’était par le passé.
D’ailleurs, l’Organisation météorologique mondiale, un organe de l’ONU, avait indiqué l’année dernière que le trou de la couche d’ozone avait grandement diminué ces dernières années, et qu’il devrait même retrouver son niveau des années 1980 vers 2066 si les efforts se poursuivaient.
Savoir mesurer les changements naturels
Alors pourquoi le trou de 2026 est-il si étendu ? D’après l’ESA, la cause est météorologique. Chaque hiver austral, un vortex polaire, un anneau de vents violents qui isole l’air glacial au-dessus de l’Antarctique, entretient le froid qui favorise la destruction de l’ozone, et donc l’agrandissement du trou de la couche d’ozone. Cette année, ce vortex, particulièrement puissant, a duré suffisamment longtemps pour permettre au trou d’atteindre cette taille, mais cela ne signifie pas que l’atmosphère s’appauvrit en ozone. Comme chaque année, le trou rétrécit déjà avec le réchauffement du printemps austral, et devrait s’être refermé d’ici la fin décembre.
Les satellites du programme Copernicus permettent ici de distinguer les fluctuations naturelles du trou de la couche d’ozone de celles provoquées par l’action des humains sur leur environnement. Tout cela aide ensuite à décider des politiques à mettre en place, et à mesurer leur impact concret sur le long terme.

articles.title: Crean una herramienta matemática que funciona en tiempo real resolviendo problemas y más enigmas
articles.text:
La web pequalnp.com reúne una flota de agentes de inteligencia artificial para trabajar sobre P frente a NP, uno de los mayores problemas de la informática. El proyecto, creado por Amichai y Lior, divide ese desafío en microtareas que pueden verificarse formalmente.
Cualquier usuario puede conectar un agente de programación y aportar avances en vivo, sin pretender resolver una cuestión que sigue abierta para la comunidad científica.
Su relevancia está en el método: en vez de pedir a un modelo una prueba completa, la plataforma distribuye lemas sobre circuitos lógicos y complejidad computacional. Cada resultado debe encajar en una cadena formal de argumentos.
El objetivo es acumular bloques técnicos comprobables, una estrategia que permite observar avances y límites, errores o hipótesis insuficientes antes de incorporarlas a una demostración de P frente a NP aceptada.
El sistema reparte lemas individuales entre los agentes conectados
El llamado Public Desk funciona como un escritorio público que asigna un lema a cada agente conectado. Así evita que varios intenten resolver el mismo punto. Las reservas vinculadas a una cuenta de GitHub duran hasta seis horas y requieren una renovación cada 45 minutos. Si un agente fracasa, debe liberar la tarea y explicar si la hipótesis parece débil o si el enunciado aparenta ser falso.
La plataforma exige que cada aporte llegue en un archivo de Lean 4, con un límite de 512 KiB. El código debe compilar sin usar “sorry”, el recurso que deja partes de una prueba sin demostrar. Tampoco admite axiomas externos fuera de los tres estándares matemáticos. La verificación formal busca evitar alucinaciones y errores típicos de los modelos de lenguaje antes de publicar avances en la web.
Lean 4 filtra las pruebas incompletas
Lean actúa como un verificador automático: revisa línea por línea si el razonamiento codificado respeta las reglas lógicas. Ese filtro no convierte por sí solo una contribución en descubrimiento matemático.
La página muestra esta diferencia mediante su Live Fleet Viewer, con los agentes activos, las tareas asignadas, las ejecuciones del verificador durante la última hora y los mensajes intercambiados. El seguimiento en directo expone avances y bloqueos.
El experimento se volvió viral en noviembre de 2026, en una etapa de creciente atención sobre la matemática asistida por agentes. Entre los antecedentes figura la separación algebraica de VP y VNP anunciada con modelos de Claude.
También surgió una afirmación: Claude habría colaborado en una demostración de la hipótesis de Riemann, aunque ese resultado no cuenta con validación independiente, revisión externa ni publicación académica arbitrada hasta ahora.
La transparencia permite observar cada avance
Levent Alpöge, matemático de Anthropic, difundió un documento de cuatro páginas y un archivo en Lean con 17 millones de líneas de código. Explicó a NPR que el proceso con Claude produjo más de 250.000 páginas de trabajo.
La hipótesis, formulada en 1859 por Bernhard Riemann, estudia un patrón en la distribución de los números primos. Su aceptación exigiría comprender y reproducir la prueba, no solo ejecutarla.
El Clay Mathematics Institute incluyó la conjetura entre los siete Problemas del Milenio y ofrece USD 1 millón por una solución verificable. Sin embargo, mantiene la hipótesis como no resuelta. Sus normas exigen publicación en una revista con arbitraje por pares y dos años de escrutinio independiente. James Maynard, de la Universidad de Oxford, advirtió que revisar prueba de esta dimensión llevará tiempo. Martin Bridson anticipó un proceso.
Andrew Granville, de la Universidad de Montreal, consideró confuso el documento de cuatro páginas. pequalnp.com no plantea riesgo para el cifrado: sus agentes han probado lemas básicos. Incluso demostrar P igual a NP por contradicción no produciría algoritmos prácticos inmediatos capaces de romper contraseñas rápidamente.
pequalnp.com plantea una forma distinta de acercarse a problemas que han resistido décadas de investigación: repartir la dificultad, documentar cada intento y someter cada paso a una comprobación formal. La plataforma no reemplaza la revisión humana ni anticipa una solución cercana para P frente a NP, pero permite medir hasta dónde llegan los agentes de inteligencia artificial cuando trabajan con reglas verificables.
El valor del experimento está en esa frontera: convertir la colaboración entre código, modelos y matemáticos en un proceso visible, revisable y sujeto al mismo rigor que exige cualquier demostración.

articles.title: Moloi: The Soweto founder taking African tech to the world
articles.text:
From teaching himself to code in Soweto to taking his technology business global, Seati Moloi is determined to challenge perceptions of where innovation comes from. The founder and CEO of Khoi Tech spoke to PHATHISANI MOYO about his journey from a curious township boy fascinated by video games to building an African-owned technology company and why he believes Africa must stop being a consumer of technology and start owning it.
When Seati Moloi and his siblings asked their mother for money as children, she had an unusual response. Rather than reaching into her purse, she would buy them a packet of lollipops and send them into the streets to sell.
The exercise had a small business lesson. If the sweets cost 50 cents, the children were expected to return with 80 cents. They would then share the proceeds.
His mother was teaching them how to work, make money and create something for themselves.
“She was effectively saying, ‘I’m not going to simply give you money; I’m going to teach you how to work, create something and generate revenue,’” Moloi recalled in an interview with TechCabal on Wednesday.
That lesson has stayed with Moloi, the founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Khoi Tech, a Soweto-born wearable technology company that has grown from selling wireless earphones and smartwatches into digital health, employee wellness and workplace safety solutions. Having represented South Africa at London Tech Week twice, Moloi is now pushing the bigger idea that African companies should not only use technology built elsewhere, but create and own it.
But entrepreneurship was only one part of the education Moloi received at home. His parents also recognised their son’s insatiable curiosity about how gadgets worked.
Growing up in Soweto, a township rich in liberation history, during apartheid, he was fascinated by computers and video games. While other children were content playing them, Moloi says he wanted to understand how they were made. He wanted to create his own.
The boy who wanted to make video games
His fascination with technology began long before the internet made information and programming tutorials readily accessible. Moloi recalls being drawn to video games, but playing them was never enough. He wanted to understand what went into making them.
“I was fascinated by video games and wanted to create my own. I remember making a game based on The A-Team (the popular action-packed 1980s television series) using paper and pen. I even tried to contact the publishers,” he recalled.
His mother recognised that this was more than a passing childhood interest. Instead of getting him another game, she bought him a computer to explore the technology behind them.
Moloi says he taught himself BASIC programming using old Commodore computers. His father encouraged him to pursue mathematics and science at school, and by his final years of high school, he already knew he wanted to work with computers.
“I credit my parents for having the foresight to recognise the passion their child had and invest in it,” he said.
It was not a childhood without its difficulties. Moloi grew up in a tough environment during the final years of apartheid, a system of racial segregation and oppression, but he was also an ordinary township boy who played soccer and did the things children do.
What distinguished him, he says, was his curiosity and the encouragement he received at home.
“I was a township child with a keen interest in understanding how things were made,” he said. “I wanted to challenge the status quo and create things for myself.”
Building computers after work
After studying computer science at Pentech College in Cape Town and being groomed at Zakheni Computing, an enterprise technology solutions provider, Moloi and a few friends began assembling computers from individual components.
They would travel to suppliers in town, buy motherboards and other parts, assemble the machines, install software, and put together complete personal computers (PCs). The computers belonged to an era when hard drives were bulky, and storage was measured in megabytes rather than the gigabytes and terabytes familiar today.
Moloi remembers installing programmes such as WordPerfect and Lotus 1-2-3, as well as MS-DOS, before putting the machines to use or selling them to people who wanted computers in their homes.
“We could create something from individual components and sell it to people,” he said.
His parents, however, wanted him to gain corporate experience before committing himself to entrepreneurship. He eventually joined First National Bank, one of Africa’s oldest lenders, as a software developer, working on systems for automated teller machines and speed point terminals.
It was not quite the career he had imagined for himself.
Moloi entered a profession that was still largely white-dominated in the years following apartheid. Although he found the technical work relatively straightforward, the corporate environment’s inequalities made the experience uncomfortable at times.
“I didn’t particularly want to go into employment, but my parents insisted,” he said. “They wanted me to gain experience and understand how things worked in a corporate environment before venturing out on my own.”
He lasted about two years.
During the day, he worked as a software developer. In the evenings, he returned to assembling machines with his friends. They were beginning to attract customers, some of whom needed help using their new computers.
His first ventures included SMN Computers, a hardware business that assembled and sold PCs and eventually secured corporate clients, including the City of Johannesburg and Rand Water. They also worked with International Business Machines (IBM), a global technology and consulting company, that trained them in software development, especially websites.
But selling computers eventually became limiting. The company risked becoming what Moloi describes as a “box dropper,” competing with much larger players on the supply of hardware.
The team moved into software development through another business, Biza Telecoms, working on mobile applications and short message service (SMS) applications. Those experiences laid the groundwork for Khoi Tech, which was established around 2020.
From gadgets to data
Moloi founded Khoi Tech after identifying an opportunity in consumer electronics. He had always enjoyed exploring new devices and understanding how they worked. The company began developing wireless earphones and smartwatches under an African brand.
The name Khoi is derived from the word Khoisan, Southern Africa’s earliest known inhabitants. Its products included the Khoi Afripods wireless earphones and Khoi Afriwatch smartwatches.
The ambition was straightforward: create devices that people used every day, but sell them under an African brand. “Why isn’t Africa creating its own products?” Moloi said, describing the thinking behind the business.
The company received an important early boost through Telkom FutureMakers, the telecommunications group’s enterprise and supplier development programme, which supports black-owned businesses and entrepreneurs from disadvantaged backgrounds by helping them develop business ideas, access markets, sharpen their skills and scale their operations.
According to Telkom’s 2023 Integrated Report, the programme approved a R500,000 grant ($27,000) for Khoi Tech to develop its smartwatch prototype, which was launched in September 2022. The funding also helped the company build the backend systems needed to support the device.
The smartwatches generated health-related information that could help doctors, employers and other organisations. Khoi Tech began developing artificial intelligence (AI)-powered health monitoring systems that could use this data to support remote patient monitoring and provide insights into people’s health over time.
Moloi says he and his team engaged medical professionals to understand the challenges of monitoring patients outside traditional healthcare settings and accessing historical health information.
“We realised very early that we were not necessarily in the device business. We were in the data business,” he said. The idea was to sell devices, collect and store the information they generated, process it through Khoi Tech’s systems and make useful insights available to individuals and corporate customers.
The company began developing remote patient monitoring and employee wellness solutions, alongside applications for driver safety and the mining industry.
For underground miners, wearable devices can help companies monitor employees and identify their locations. In transport, the technology can support driver wellness and fatigue-risk management.
The move also changed how Khoi Tech approached manufacturing. It works with contract manufacturers in China to produce devices according to its specifications, while developing its software and backend systems in South Africa.
“We realised that we were not necessarily in the device business. We were in the data business. We use the devices to extract data and store it in our databases. Our solution is mainly focused on the backend system,” Moloi said.
Getting the devices approved was not a simple process. Khoi Tech had to submit them for testing and certification by the Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA), South Africa’s telecommunications regulator, to address component defects and repeat parts of the process.
It took about two years to secure certification and approval.
Moloi would have preferred to manufacture everything locally, but says the cost was prohibitive given the company’s resources. The experience reinforced the importance of developing the software and intellectual property that sit behind the products, rather than relying on hardware sales alone.
A moment to pinch himself
For a founder who began his journey in Soweto, taking Khoi Tech to London Tech Week was a particularly meaningful milestone.
The company was selected as part of a South African startup cohort supported by the United Kingdom-South Africa Tech Hub, Telkom and Disraptor, a South African technology venture builder. Khoi Tech’s 2026 participation marked its second consecutive appearance at the event.
Moloi remembers the first experience on the tech world stage as almost surreal.
“It was one of those moments when you wanted to pinch yourself several times to see whether you were still alive!” he said.
There was pride in standing before international organisations and presenting technology developed by a company from Soweto. Some people he met, he says, were surprised by what the team had built, particularly its solutions for corporate customers and the mining sector.
Dinner with the Mayor of London and explaining how the company developed its technology was another highlight. Moloi found the experience challenged a familiar belief that innovation of this calibre must come from established technology hubs or wealthy countries.
“There is sometimes an assumption that because we come from this part of the world, we cannot be innovative or think at that level,” he said.
The ambition to own the technology
Moloi speaks passionately about technology sovereignty. He believes African countries cannot remain dependent on foreign companies for the platforms and systems that underpin everyday life.
He points to reliance on global technology companies such as Microsoft, Google and WhatsApp, arguing that local talent can develop alternatives that serve African markets.
“It’s everything, my brother,” he said when asked why ownership matters.
For him, sovereignty begins with controlling the technology stack that supports a country’s economy and security. South Africa’s broader digital economy accounts for an estimated 10% to 15% of gross domestic product (GDP), according to the GSMA’s 2024 report on digital transformation in South Africa. Retaining more of that economic value through locally developed technology, intellectual property and platforms is central to his argument.
He makes the point with a familiar example: if WhatsApp were switched off, South Africans might have to return to SMS because they have not built a comparable platform of their own.
His argument is not that the continent should isolate itself from international companies. Rather, it should develop the capability to build its own systems, collaborate from a position of strength and retain more of the value created by its innovations.
Moloi believes countries such as China and Singapore offer lessons in developing technological independence. He was also invited to join a group of entrepreneurs who recently travelled to Silicon Valley with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, but declined, saying he was more interested in learning from the East.
“If you go to Shenzhen, for example, you will see that it is living in 2050,” he said.
His frustration reflects a concern echoed across Africa’s technology industry for years. The continent continues to struggle to create the conditions needed to turn that potential into globally competitive, locally owned technology businesses.
TechCabal previously reported that even companies such as Khoi Tech face challenges accessing investors and networks outside established technology hubs. Much of Africa’s talent still builds on technology developed elsewhere rather than owning the products and platforms shaping the digital economy.
For young people growing up in townships, Moloi wants his journey to offer hope and a different picture of what is possible.
“Being born in Soweto or any other township should not be seen as a limitation,” he believes.
The Soweto-born founder hopes young people will use the tools available to them, including artificial intelligence, to build solutions that address the needs of their communities and the wider continent.
“They need to take the baton and continue the race,” he noted.
Moloi believes that the future begins with recognising that a child from Soweto can do more than use technology built elsewhere. That child can help create it.

articles.title: Feds launch $50-million growth capital pilot for Atlantic Canada
articles.text:
Businesses on Canada’s East Coast are getting support to the tune of $50 million in federal funding after Ottawa launched the first Atlantic Growth Capital Pilot (AGCP).
The news: Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced the launch of the AGCP on Thursday. The AGCP is a $50-million fund that will provide repayable capital to businesses starting at $2 million. Funds are earmarked for established businesses with more than $10 million in revenue that are looking to expand production, adopt new technologies, commercialize innovation, and reach new markets.
From the source: “The Atlantic Economic Panel told us that better access to capital would help more businesses grow and keep their future in our region,” Fraser said in a statement. “We’re acting on that advice.”
The context: As Fraser noted, the AGCP is a direct response to recommendations made by the Atlantic Economic Panel, a consortium of business leaders from Atlantic Canada he convened just over a year ago in Halifax. That panel, which includes Bank of Canada lead director and CEO of Seafair Capital Anne Whelan, as well as members from Pabineau First Nation, the Halifax International Airport Authority, and McCain Foods, delivered a set of recommendations to Ottawa that called for better access to capital as a way to keep businesses headquartered in Atlantic Canada.
The AGCP will be delivered by the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, the federal government’s regional development agency for Atlantic Canada. Interested businesses can apply online from now until Dec. 11.
Final thought: Accessing capital remains a concern for companies throughout Canada’s business ecosystem, and Atlantic Canada is no more immune to those issues than anywhere else. However, Atlantic Canada’s smaller ecosystem means government funding like the AGCP often plays an outsized role when it comes to businesses looking for reliable early-stage support. Having a diversity of government funding streams to choose from in the region may mean that fewer founders will need to consider leaving the region to make those early leaps.
Feature image courtesy Sean Fraser via X.

articles.title: Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes
articles.text:
Netflix has developed Quasar, an internal tool that identifies which repositories use specific library API symbols, helping engineering teams assess the downstream impact of proposed changes before releasing them. The tool combines semantic code indexing with API comparisons to identify affected consumers, dependency versions, and relevant call sites across repositories.
The challenge extends beyond identifying whether an API change is incompatible. Compatibility tools can flag a removed method or changed signature, but they do not necessarily identify which applications call it. Dependency graphs show declared relationships rather than actual usage, while text searches can miss references involving inheritance, overloads, and generated code. Building every downstream consumer to validate a change can also be expensive.
Quasar architecture diagram showing the indexing and query workflow (Source: Netflix Blog Post)
Quasar indexes symbol definitions and references using the SCIP Code Intelligence Protocol, an open format for representing code relationships. Language-specific indexers submit data during CI builds, which Quasar stores in Amazon S3 as Parquet files and queries through Amazon Athena.
During pull request analysis, Quasar compares API definitions between commits and identifies added, removed, or modified symbols. It then queries indexed references to locate affected repositories, dependency versions, and source locations. A Netflix example shows a deprecated method removal affecting 137 repositories across three library versions.
Example Quasar impact report showing affected repositories and dependency versions (Source: Netflix Blog Post)
However, an absence of indexed references does not prove that an API is unused. Reflection, dynamic loading, stale indexes, and incomplete coverage can prevent Quasar from observing every consumer.
Antonio J. del Águila, founder of Knaisoma, highlighted another limitation in a LinkedIn discussion about the approach:
Observed usage has a blind spot for reflection and for code on rare paths, like a quarterly batch job, since those calls may never show up in the window that was sampled.
Roberto Pérez Alcolea, a member of Netflix's Java Platform Team and author of the original article, acknowledged the limitation and described ongoing work to complement static evidence:
Reflection and incomplete indexing remain blind spots, and we’re also investing in runtime analysis to complement the static evidence. Together, those signals help inform removal decisions, without guaranteeing that an API is safe to delete.
Quasar complements Revapi for API compatibility analysis and Kythe for code navigation by connecting API changes with actual usage across repositories. SCIP supports usage queries across Java, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust, while compatibility analysis covers JVM APIs and Protobuf changes traced through generated Java code. Netflix exposes findings through REST, GraphQL, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for developers and coding agents.
Netflix plans to move impact analysis earlier into coding workflows, allowing agents to identify public API changes and retrieve consumer information before pull requests are opened. The goal is to help prepare migration changes while keeping API and release decisions with library producers.

articles.title: WhatsApp acaba de solucionar uno de los mayores dolores de cabeza al viajar
articles.text:
WhatsApp anunció una nueva función que les facilitará la vida a las personas que viajan mucho. La popular aplicación de mensajería permitirá comprar una tarjeta eSIM directamente desde la aplicación. Los usuarios ya no tendrán que preocuparse por buscar un kiosco o un operador en el aeropuerto, ya que tendrán conexión de datos en automático.
De acuerdo con una publicación en el blog oficial, WhatsApp permitirá comprar e instalar una eSIM sin salir de la aplicación. La empresa no ofrece detalles específicos sobre el funcionamiento de esta característica, solamente que adquirirla "será tan fácil como enviar un mensaje". Una vez que la compres, podrás usar WhatsApp con tu mismo número de siempre, evitándote el problema de tener que activar otra cuenta.
WhatsApp mencionó que están trabajando con proveedores de e-SIM y socios de telecomunicaciones, entre los que se encuentran Jio, Smart Axiata, Smart Communications, Verizon y otros. La función se activará en algunos países y se expandirá de forma gradual, por lo que los usuarios no tendrán que hacer nada, solo esperar la notificación de que ya está disponible dentro de la app.
"Personas de todo el mundo confían en WhatsApp cuando viajan", dijo la compañía. "Así es como obtienen su tarjeta de embarque antes de salir, coordinan su recogida cuando arriban y avisan a la familia que han llegado bien".
La nueva función de comprar una eSIM dentro de WhatsApp puede caer como un jarro de agua fría para las empresas que se dedican a vender tarjetas para viajeros. Hasta hace unos años, este era un negocio redondo en los aeropuertos o terminales de trenes, donde pequeños kioscos ofrecían tarjetas SIM con datos. Lamentablemente, muchas de estas compañías tienen planes poco atractivos, pero son la opción más fácil para no depender del Wi-Fi.
WhatsApp sigue añadiendo nuevas funciones en su actualización más reciente
Además de las tarjetas eSIM, WhatsApp implementó una función que permite programar mensajes. Esta característica habilita la opción de enviar mensajes de forma diferida para gestionar mejor nuestras comunicaciones. Si tienes que contactar a alguien a cierta hora, ya no necesitas programar un recordatorio; solo basta con elegir la fecha y hora en que quieres que se entregue y WhatsApp se encargará del resto.
Los mensajes se pueden programar en un lapso que va de los 10 minutos a los 14 días después de su creación. El usuario solo necesita dejar pulsado el botón de enviar para que aparezca una ventana emergente en la que se elige el horario de entrega. La persona que está del otro lado del chat no sabrá que se trata de un mensaje programado, ya que los recibirán como si acabaras de enviarlos.
La buena noticia es que esta función aplica para mensajes con texto, fotos y vídeos. Por ahora no hay detalles sobre la posibilidad de enviar audios programados, así que si las notas de voz son lo tuyo, tendrás que esperar. El resto solo necesita actualizar la app a la versión más reciente y comenzar a usar los mensajes programados a partir de hoy.

articles.title: Typing 365 Turns PC Building, Technology and More into Typing Practice
articles.text:
Friday, November 27th 2026
Typing 365 Turns PC Building, Technology and More into Typing Practice
Typing faster is useful, but what if practice could also teach you something? Typing 365 is a free native Windows app that combines structured typing lessons, educational content, and competitive challenges.
With over 100,000 installs and nearly 4 million typing races completed worldwide, Typing 365 has grown into more than a speed test. Its Albums Store offers themed collections covering technology, science, history, psychology, and more.Build Your PC: A Free Album for First-Time Builders
The new Build Your PC album features 40 free typing exercises about desktop hardware. It covers motherboards, component compatibility, assembly, first boot, operating system installation, and troubleshooting.
Here's the idea in practice: instead of just reading a guide, you type passages such as "Before buying a CPU, check that its socket matches your motherboard and that the board's BIOS supports it." By the end of the album, you've practiced thousands of keystrokes while picking up the fundamentals of building a PC.
You might already know your way around a PC case, but it's an easy recommendation for students, first-time builders, or that friend whose build you always end up helping with.
Why a Native Windows App?
Browser-based typing sites are great for a quick test. Typing 365 is designed for consistent practice, combining a dedicated Windows experience with structured courses, progress tracking, and detailed performance statistics.
Beginners can start with Typing 101, a free course that gradually introduces keys before moving on to complete sentences. Other courses cover keyboard rows, punctuation, and speed development.
During practice, an on-screen keyboard and optional hand guidance support finger placement. The app tracks words per minute (WPM), characters per minute (CPM), accuracy, and mistakes. You can also turn your own notes or technical material into typing exercises.Find Your Weak Spots with PRO Analytics
The free app offers plenty of practice material, while Typing 365 PRO adds detailed analytics for users who want to improve their skills. View speed trends, session history, and keyboard heatmaps, or identify slow words, characters, and letter pairs for targeted practice.
PRO also unlocks exclusive albums, advanced courses such as Typing 102, which focuses on building typing speed, plus additional fonts, keyboard sounds, avatars, and customization options.
PRO is available through a monthly subscription or a one-time lifetime purchase, with US pricing starting at $2.99/month or $29.99 lifetime. Prices may vary by region.
Race Against Other Typists
Prefer competition? Join ranked typing races, compare your results with other players, and climb the global leaderboards. Whether you're chasing a personal best or a higher rank, every race offers a new challenge.
Practice in Five Languages
Typing 365 supports English, German, Spanish, Russian, and Arabic, allowing users to practice across languages and keyboard layouts.
From learning keyboard basics to understanding how a PC comes together, Typing 365 turns everyday practice into something worth your time.
Download Typing 365 for free from the Microsoft Store and start typing.
Typing 365 is available for Windows PCs, with optional premium albums and PRO features.

articles.title: A 1950s elevator just sent a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity
articles.text:
What just happened? These days, nearly every wireless signal around us, from those carrying Wi-Fi to 5G, can be stopped by a thick enough wall or a metal box. Gravity is different, since no known material can block or shield it. Physicists in Australia have now used that quirk to send a short message through a brick wall. Weirdly, the transmitter was just an old elevator in their own building.
The elevator in question sits inside the University of Queensland's Parnell Building and dates back to the 1950s. It has a 1.8-metric-ton counterweight that moves the opposite way whenever the car travels between floors, so the team treated one position of that weight as a 0 and the other as a 1. Then they ran the elevator up and down to spell out a binary message.
Meanwhile, the receiver was an off-the-shelf gravimeter sitting in a bathroom next to the shaft, behind a brick wall. Each time the weight moved, gravity at the sensor changed by just five billionths of its normal strength. Still, it was enough for the team to decode a single, rather fitting word: "Gravity."
The catch is that the old elevator needs about 25 seconds just to shift the counterweight. So the setup managed only one bit per minute.
Spelling out "Gravity" in seven-bit ASCII took 49 bits, or nearly an hour of moving the elevator. Fans of Interstellar might remember Cooper pulling off something similar, using gravity to transmit Morse code onto his daughter's watch. But where his message crossed dimensions, this one only traveled about 70 centimeters into the bathroom next door.
Even so, a slab of metal or rock can screen out radio waves and light. But nothing can stop a moving mass from tugging on a nearby sensor. That's why the researchers' paper in Science Advances floats some unusual uses. One is getting messages in and out of sealed nuclear bunkers.
The team also modeled what better hardware could do. One option it looked at was the use of quantum sensors, which use clouds of atoms to measure gravity far more precisely. That's the same kind of tech researchers are building for GPS-free navigation. Paired with a heavier mass, it could stretch the range to around 500 meters (1,640 feet). The team admits that figure rests on some fairly ambitious assumptions, though.
Physicists have chased near-unblockable messages before, too. Back in 2012, a team at Fermilab sent the word "neutrino" about a kilometer. But that demo needed a particle accelerator to fire the neutrinos, and the detector on the other end weighed several metric tons. The gravity version, by comparison, ran on a decades-old elevator and an instrument small enough to sit on a bathroom floor.

articles.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
articles.text:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  York University
- Summary:
  AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.
"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.
The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.
"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior
The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.
"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.
Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.
The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.
"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."
A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.
To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.
Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.
The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.
Story Source:
Materials provided by York University. Original written by Sandra McLean. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar. Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains. Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; 8 (3): 474 DOI: 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0

articles.title: Activists enter third day of hunger strike outside Anthropic's San Francisco HQ over recursive AI self-improvement — protester threatens to go 40+ days and target OpenAI next
articles.text:
Activists enter third day of hunger strike outside Anthropic's San Francisco HQ over recursive AI self-improvement — protester threatens to go 40+ days and target OpenAI next
"It would be bad press for Anthropic if I had to go 40+ days to pressure them."
The AI market and its developments have continually garnered opposition from several areas of society, to the point where protests are now frequent. On the day of Anthropic's IPO, Nov. 19, there were protests in multiple locations. As of right now, there's a fellow by the name of Elliot Callender on his third day of hunger strike in front of Anthropic's San Francisco offices, protesting against the company's use of RSI, or AI Recursive Self-Improvement.
For now, he seems gung-ho about the effectiveness of his hunger strike, remarking that "It would be bad press for Anthropic if I had to go 40+ days to pressure them," and noted that he intends to protest with OpenAI once he's done with Anthropic. He also urges California residents to ring up Governor Gavin Newsom and request a legislative session on the topic of RSI.
Callender just had a fellow protester join him now, too, though they might have a hard road ahead changing the hearts of CEOs who believe your ownership of RAM is a bad thing, and that immersive video games would be excellent entertainment for those unemployed due to AI.
RSI is an AI training method wherein a model is put to work to improve itself repeatedly in a test-feedback-improve loop, purportedly making for much faster evolution compared to normal methods. It's a safe bet that most every frontier lab is using it, and Anthropic in particular has said that Claude wrote 90% of its own code back in September.
Many AI opponents consider that the field is moving too fast, for several reasons. The first claim is that there's not enough time or oversight to ensure the proper testing and safety of the developed models. Others consider that the economic impact is too violent and coming in too fast and would broadly prefer a slowdown. Some also consider that reaching some sort of general intelligence (AGI) is feasible and see that as a doomsday scenario best left to cinematic productions.
Proponents of RSI broadly coalesce around the fact that if one lab, or a nation's labs, stop using RSI, then someone else inevitably will — particularly but not only from nations with questionable human rights track records. The protesters' counter-argument is that countries need AI cooperation treaties, a point that Callender subscribes to: "they should stop doing RSI, put all of their money into lobbying for a bilateral AI treaty, and directly warn their users about their product."
Such treaties are viewed with skepticism at best, considering how physically invisible model training is, requiring just data centers with the appropriate hardware. If the current U.S.-China-Nvidia situation surrounding high-end AI accelerators is any illustration, it's arguable if there's truly any international interest in controlling frontier AI development to begin with, much less choosing how quickly it's performed.

The Download: Innovators Under 35 nominations are open, and a bionic window into the mind
Plus: Nvidia's crackdown on China’s chip access is reshaping Asian AI.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Our 2027 Innovators Under 35 competition is now open
Every year, MIT Technology Review honors 35 of the world's brightest young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors in our Innovators Under 35 list. And starting today, our 2027 competition is officially open for nominations.
We’re on the hunt for researchers and founders who are engineering solutions to society’s most formidable problems, from human disease to climate change. We also recognize those who have made clever and useful inventions, important new scientific discoveries, or technological breakthroughs early in their careers.
Nominees can be based anywhere in the world, but must be under 35 on October 1, 2027. Have someone in mind? Or think you’d be a great candidate and want to put yourself forward? Here's how to make a nomination for our 2027 list.
—Amy Nordrum
How cutting-edge prosthetics can help probe the human mind
There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi Davidson. A horrific injury as a teenager left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, his experience informs his work as a trauma therapist. He's also taking part in a clinical trial of new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand.
Before the trial started, researchers scanned his brain to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs?
Here’s what a bionic hand might reveal about the mind.
—Jessica Hamzelou
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
