articles.title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
articles.text:
Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
This essay originally appeared in The Guardian. It’s an expanded version of the one I posted as “We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For.”
It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.
The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.
None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.
Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.
A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.
There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problems lie.
Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.
Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies—and, additionally, all other positive intangibles—out of a company in pursuit of those profits.
Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.
From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful until something bad happens.
But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.
The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes.
The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.
Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.
We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation—with enforcement and meaningful fines—and stringent antitrust enforcement.
But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement—especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.
Rontea • November 27, 2026 8:38 AM
From an operational security and resilience standpoint, this aligns with what we often see in critical infrastructure: complex systems with many interdependencies and latent fragility. When budgets prioritize efficiency and short-term return, redundant architectures, robust incident response planning, and thorough testing are often treated as optional luxuries. That approach works—until it doesn’t. Each high-profile outage reinforces a lesson we’ve learned repeatedly: resilience isn’t free, and it has to be built in before the crisis, not after.

articles.title: The absolute best Black Friday deals you can still get
articles.text:
Black Friday is nearly over, but many of this year’s best deals are still available. You can still find some of the lowest prices we’ve seen in-store and online for video games, wireless earbuds, TVs, robot vacuums, and so much more. We can’t guarantee a deal you’ve had your eye on will last through Cyber Monday; however, if prior years are any indication, most will stick around through the long weekend.
The absolute best Black Friday deals you can still get
Many of our favorite gadgets and gizmos are cheaper than they’ve been all year, making now the perfect time to shop.
As usual, we sorted through thousands of deals to find the ones truly worth sharing, with an eye for the products and services we’ve tested here at The Verge. With prices up across multiple categories due to RAMageddon, some deals may not seem as big as in prior years. For example, Apple’s latest MacBook Air recently fell to its pre-price-hike level for the first time since July. That’s a deal to us, and several other discounts are still taking a similar shape, even as Black Friday draws to a close.
AirPods Pro 3
Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.
Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle
You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.
Anker Universal Charger (100W)
Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.
Xteink X4 Classic pocket e-reader
With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering; it also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.
Nintendo Switch 2 + Mario Kart World Bundle
The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.
HBO Max
An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.
Eufy Omni C28
The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.
SwitchBot Bot Rechargeable
Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.
Kodak Charmera Keychain Digital Camera
The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage.
Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5)
Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.
Octobuddy Classic
Who needs magnets when you have suction cups? Octobuddy’s cheap silicone mount works with most phones to provide hands-free flexibility whenever necessary. It features 24 single-sided cups, which allow you to stick your phone to a mirror, window, or any other surface you think will provide that perfect TikTok angle.
Peacock
Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and DreamWorks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.
Samsung P9 microSD Express card
The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.
Fanttik X9 Pro Portable Tire Inflator
The Fanttik X9 Pro can inflate a car tire in under a minute, making routine maintenance fast and easy. There are four one-click presets for cars, motorcycles, bikes, and balls, along with a manual mode that reaches a maximum pressure of 150PSI.
Apple iPad (11th generation)
Apple’s 11th-gen iPad follows up the 10th-gen model with a new A16 chip and few other changes — and is the only Apple tablet to not support Apple Intelligence.
Anker 140W 2-in-1 USB-C to USB-C Cable
No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.
Paramount Plus (monthly subscription)
Paramount Plus Premium provides access to live sports as well as movies and shows from both platforms, including Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a host of Yellowstone spinoffs, Star Trek shows, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, Twin Peaks, Dexter, and more.
Sony WH-1000XM4C
Sony’s XM4 noise-canceling headphones were so good, the company brought them back with a few minor improvements. They still offer great ANC, a timeless foldable design, and delivering performance nearly on par with Sony’s newer flagships at a fraction of the cost.
Govee Table Lamp 2
Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.
Kindle Paperwhite (2024)
Compared to the last-gen base Kindle model (currently $119.99), the Paperwhite is a much better value. It features waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher-pixel-density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches).
Noco GB40 UltraSafe Jumpstarter
Noco’s Boost GB40 is a rechargeable battery with jumper cables to start six-liter gas or three-liter diesel engines. It also has USB ports so you can charge your phone, ensuring you always have a backup plan.
Oura Ring 5
The Ring 5 is a fantastic entry point for new users. While short on improvements over its thicker predecessor, it’s hard not to appreciate that it manages to deliver similar battery life despite being thinner. Read our review.
Sonos Play
The water-resistant Sonos Play sits between the Roam 2 and Move 2, offering a balance of portability and room-filling sound. It delivers up to 24 hours of battery life, with a built-in loop for easy carrying. You can also use it as a power bank and pair it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when Wi-Fi isn’t available. Read our review.
Zepath USB-C Li-ion AA Batteries
Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.
007 First Light
007 First Light, a third-person stealth action game from the studio behind Hitman, is one of the best action games we’ve played this year. It features a wide variety of missions that have you sneaking through enemy territory, engaging in hand-to-hand combat, and taking part in high-speed car chases — you know, classic Bond stuff. Read our review.
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus
Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.
Fanttik S1 Pro Cordless Electric Screwdriver
Fanttik’s rechargeable electric screwdriver features three adjustable torque settings, a built-in LED light, and 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling everything from furniture assembly to small electronics repairs. It also comes with a magnetic storage case and supports USB-C.
Apple TV (six-month subscription)
Apple TV offers ad-free streaming of original shows and movies, including shows like Severance, Silo, Slow Horses, and Pluribus. The service also features a rotating selection of films, along with live Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.
Apple Watch Series 12
The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.
Anker Laptop Power Bank
Anker’s 25,000mAh power bank sports two built-in USB-C cables (one of which is retractable), plus one USB-C and USB-A port. It tops out at 165W when charging two devices simultaneously, or 130W when charging three or four.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
The cost continues to fall on Samsung’s latest, best foldable yet. The Z Fold 8 is a passport-style phone, like the iPhone Duo, with fast performance and slick design.
Nothing Ear 3A earbuds
You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review.
Acer Swift Air 14
Acer’s answer to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Core 5 processor, 8GB of RAM, 120Hz display, and speedy Thunderbolt 4 ports. We’re still testing this one, but it’s showing promise for an affordable choice.
Lego Project Hail Mary set
Outside of the Integrity, few spacecraft made as big a splash in 2026 as the one Ryland Grace piloted in Project Hail Mary. And now, thanks to Lego, you can construct a microscale replica of the titular Hail Mary, complete with a miniature Rocky figure.
Hoto 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro
Hoto’s rechargeable screwdriver is ideal for small repairs. It offers three torque modes, a rotational speed of up to 220RPM, and a helpful circular LED to illuminate dark spaces. The durable case also holds all 25 steel bits and an extension bar for getting into hard-to-reach places.
Sony DualSense Wireless Controller
Sony’s DualSense Wireless Controller for the PlayStation 5 features immersive haptic feedback and resistance triggers, which feel great to use. It offers a built-in mic, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and a mute button; it also works with PC, macOS, and mobile devices via Bluetooth or USB-C.
MacBook Neo
Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.
Ember Mug 3 (14-ounce)
Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.
LG B6E OLED TV
Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.
Alienware 32-inch 4K OLED gaming monitor
One of the most affordable Tandem RGB Stripe OLEDs is even cheaper during Black Friday. The AW3226Q monitor has a 165Hz refresh rate, G-Sync compatibility, better-looking text rendering than most other OLED monitors, and unbeatable contrast.
JBL Tour One M3
JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.
Apple Watch Ultra 4
The latest super-rugged wearable from Apple features better battery life than the previous version, plus AI-powered features like Siri Recap also available on the Series 12.
Iniu P55-E2 Power Bank (10,000mAh)
Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.
Hisense CanvasTV (2026)
Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.
Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo
The Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a beginner-friendly 3D printer that supports four filament spools. It features an enclosed build chamber, automatic bed leveling, and a large touchscreen, making it easy to produce reliable prints.
Moft Trackable Tripod Wallet
Moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.
Birdfy Feeder Metal 2 4K
Birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. It also offers free AI-powered recognition of more than 6,000 bird species.
Sharge Icemag 3 Power Bank
The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.
Saros
Saros is a third-person sci-fi shooter in which players fight alien enemies on a mysterious planet trapped in a time loop. The PS5 exclusive features fast-paced combat, a variety of powerful weapons, and challenging boss fights. Read our review.
Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2
Bose’s second-gen QuietComfort Headphones build on the original with better sound quality and support for lossless audio over USB-C. They also offer improved noise cancellation and are more comfortable thanks to their lack of “eardrum suck.”
Dreame X60 Ultra
The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.
Garmin Forerunner 265S
Garmin’s midrange Forerunner watch has an OLED display, a week’s worth of battery life, and dual-frequency GPS for better accuracy. Read our review.
Samsung The Frame (2025)
Samsung’s last-gen Frame is a 4K QLED TV that displays art on its anti-glare matte screen when not in use. It also supports Dolby Atmos, HDR10 Plus, and popular streaming apps, with refresh rates up to 144Hz on larger models.
TP-Link Tapo Matter-Certified Smart Plug Mini
TP-Link’s Wi-Fi smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms to set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.
Pixel Buds 2a
Google’s latest pair of wireless earbuds features crisp sound, a comfortable design, and solid active noise cancellation, which is great considering the budget-friendly price tag. They even offer built-in support for Gemini and, unlike the entry-level AirPods, a purple option! Read our review.
Roku Pro Series 4K OLED TV
Roku now makes some of the most affordable yet feature-packed 4K OLED TVs available for gamers or movie lovers looking for a big TV upgrade under $1,000. The Pro Series LX with better brightness, faster refresh rate, and a polarizer to reduce reflections starts at $200 more.
Alienware AW2726DM QD-OLED monitor
If you’re on a tight budget but want spectacular contrast and brightness control that only an OLED can provide, here’s a deal for you. Alienware’s 1440p 27-inch QD-OLED monitor with 240Hz refresh rate is selling at its lowest price yet. Read our hands-on.
Dell XPS 13 (2026)
The best XPS 13 in years. It doesn’t have a headphone jack and starts with only 8GB of RAM, but it’s an excellent thin-and-light with a great screen, a solid Intel chip, and speedy storage.
Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro
Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for less than Apple’s latest AirPods.
Beats Powerbeats Pro 2
The latest Powerbeats Pro are a no-brainer for athletes. They pack fantastic sound and thumping bass, along with active noise cancellation, IPX4 water resistance, and heart rate monitoring. Read our review.
Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike
The big difference between the Superstrike and other gaming mice lies beneath its main two mouse buttons. It uses haptic actuators instead of mechanical switches, allowing for lower latency and more longevity.
Yoto Mini (2024) speaker
A great first portable music player/speaker for kids. It uses insertable NFC cards (sold separately) to play music and stories to keep kiddos occupied and entertained without zoning out in front of the TV. This model supports Bluetooth and 3.5mm for private listening, too.
Nex Playground
The Nex Playground’s motion-controlled gameplay is designed for ages five and up. It comes with games like Fruit Ninja and Whack-a-Mole Deluxe, but many more titles are available via a subscription. It’s a ton of fun for kids. This is the lowest price so far in 2026. Read our review.
Apple AirPods Max (second-gen)
Nothing has changed in terms of aesthetics, but the Max 2 deliver better sound and some new features. Not exactly worth upgrading for, but fantastic for those who are considering them now. Read our full review.
Govee Uplighter Floor Lamp
It’s hard to find a cooler lamp than Govee’s Uplighter floor lamp at this price. It can light a room and display a mesmerizing pattern up your wall and onto your ceiling.
Meta Quest 3S
The Meta Quest 3S is a battery-powered standalone VR headset that has the same chipset as the pricier Quest 3, but with the same lenses and screen resolution as the Quest 2. In addition to being able to play many games from the Meta Store, it can also be connected to a gaming PC to play VR games like Half-Life Alyx. Read our review.
Ghost of Yōtei
Sucker Punch’s follow-up to Ghost of Tsushima is everything you could want in a sequel. The open-world revenge epic brims with fluid combat and a host of welcome narrative twists, all set against the gorgeous backdrop of Japan’s Edo period. It’s precisely the type of game photo modes were made for, even if you never use them.
Beats 360 headphones
The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.
Donkey Kong Bananza
Donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. Its destructible environment allows you to smash your way through each of its 17 levels, and the paths you make will remain intact unless you specifically choose to reset the world. Your companion Pauline’s singing allows you to transform into animals that have abilities that allow you to reach previously inaccessible parts of levels. Read our review.
Lego Mandalorian N-1 Starfighter
Arguably the best thing to come out of The Book of Boba Fett was the Mandalorian’s N-1 Starfighter, which Lego has re-created here in miniature. It’s not quite as impressive as the 1,802-piece version, but the cheaper set still packs plenty of detail, including a spring-loaded shooter.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive is the best way to relive what is arguably the best Zelda game of all time. The revamped visuals look gorgeous, and while the game’s improved controls might annoy some purists who still cling to the heyday of ’98, we reckon most folks won’t bat an eye.
Amazon Alexa Photo Frame
A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options, it’s a frame that features Alexa and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.
Aqara Smart Lock U400
This innovative new smart lock uses the U1 ultra-wideband (UWB) chip in many iPhones and Apple Watches to automatically unlock your door as you approach. It also works with the new Aliro standard, making it compatible with Android phones for hands-free unlocking. Read our review.
Twelve South AirFly SE
Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.
Catan (6th Edition)
In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.
Control Resonant
Control Resonant is all about manipulation — of gravity, not people. Remedy’s excellent sequel to Control is an exhilarating action game, with ever-changing combat, twisted level design, and the weirdest traversal mechanics we’ve seen in a long time.
Birdbuddy Pro (solar)
Birdbuddy’s charming, camera-equipped feeder identifies and snaps shots of each bird that stops by, supplementing its 5-megapixel stills with insightful facts via an app. The solar roof helps keep the camera’s battery topped up even when it’s cloudy outside.
Azul
Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.
Magna-Tile Classic 32-Piece Set
Magna-Tiles are a quintessential kids’ toy. The colorful, semi-translucent geometric shapes are a favorite here at The Verge, especially for those of us who prefer the simplicity of building with magnets rather than bricks.
Lego Botanicals Mini Bonsai Trees set
Lego’s 709-piece kit lets you construct three brick-ified bonsai trees, including a black pine, a ginkgo with yellow leaves, and a wisteria with hanging lilac flowers. It also comes with three ornamental displays, just in case you want a raised stand on which to showcase them.
Sonos Beam (Gen 2)
The Beam isn’t as powerful as the Sonos Arc, nor can it match the flagship soundbar’s Dolby Atmos immersion bubble. But you still get room-filling surround sound for less money — and the Beam ties into the Sonos ecosystem for added convenience. Read our review.
Google Pixel 11 Pro
Google wants to sell you on the Pro’s software features, but it’s the underlying hardware that makes it a stellar Android handset. The build quality is incredible, the larger telephoto sensor is an improvement, and it now supports faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W wireless charging. Read our review.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design. Read our review.
Insta360 Link 2
The Insta360 Link 2 offers the same auto-swiveling design as its excellent predecessor, only in a smaller form factor. It also offers a slate of new features, including group tracking and no-follow zones.
CMF Buds 2A
With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.
Philips Hue Festavia string lights
These smart lights have beautiful colors, a nice selection of festive scenes, and an easy-to-use app. They are super reliable when paired with a Hue Bridge and also work over Bluetooth. They come in three lengths, work with all the major smart home platforms, and are Matter-compatible. Read our review.
Echo Dot Max
The Echo Dot Max features a flat design and a redesigned sound system, which delivers nearly three times the bass as its predecessor. It also offers improved conversation detection and better noise filtering, thanks to Amazon’s new AZ3 chip. Read our review.
Glocusent Bookmark Style Reading Light
Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.
Vantage
Vantage isn’t your typical open-world exploration game. It’s a sci-fi roguelike that has you traversing an alien planet alongside up to five players, each of whom must solve puzzles and complete their mission before their time, morale, or health runs out. It’s not as charming as Stonemaier’s award-winning Wingspan, but it is far more interesting.
SwitchBot Standing Circulator Fan
A quiet, battery-powered fan that moves a lot of air despite its small size, the Switchbot Standing Circulator is a surprisingly versatile smart home addition.
JBL Go 4
The last-gen JBL Go 4 has been around for a bit, but the pocket-sized Bluetooth speaker still delivers with up to seven hours of runtime, dual-device connectivity, and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance. You can also pair it with other Go 4 speakers for bigger stereo sound, if desired.
Fairphone 6 Plus
Fairphone’s latest is a very light update to the 6, adding a newer processor and carrying forward its repairability and ethical values. Tradeoffs compared to a traditional smartphone are few, and the benefits are real.
Ugreen Nexode 240W USB-C Cable with Digital Display
The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). It also supports 480Mbps data transfer speeds and, unlike similar power meter-equipped cables, lets you turn off the screen when needed.
Apple Watch SE 3
The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.
Pokémon Pokopia
Nintendo’s latest Pokémon spinoff for the Switch 2 is part Pokémon, part Minecraft, and part Animal Crossing. Yet, despite borrowing gameplay mechanics from each, the cozy life sim is more than the sum of its expansive, building-centric parts. It’s breezy and warm-hearted, with enough secrets to keep you occupied for hours on end.
Google Pixel 10A
Google’s new Pixel 10A introduces faster wired charging, Satellite SOS, and new AI tools like Camera Coach and Auto Best Take. Otherwise, it’s basically the Pixel 9A, with the same Tensor G4 chip and a dual-camera system. Read our review.
Asus ProArt P14 (RTX Spark)
The entry point into RTX Spark laptops, the Asus ProArt is a creator-focused MacBook Pro wannabe with a sleek blacked-out design and lovely OLED display. Read our initial Nvidia RTX Spark hands-on.
Fractal Scape gaming headset
There are many gaming headsets out there, but few as elegant as Fractal’s Scape. The PC-focused (but Switch- and PlayStation-compatible) wireless headset offers great sound and includes a wireless charger, and it has easy-to-master physical controls.
Nintendo eShop gift cards
Everyone knows gift cards aren’t the best gift, but with such steep discounts happening on Nintendo eShop credit, you can save a lot on a Switch 2, or games and accessories, if you’re alright with jumping through a couple extra hoops.
Xreal One Pro AR glasses
USB-C display glasses can make travel (or relaxing on the couch) more fun by putting a huge virtual screen in front of your face. Xreal’s One Pro are some of the best out there at displaying content from your phone, tablet, laptop, or portable handheld.
Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2
Govee’s Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 are Matter-ready smart lights you can leave up year-round. They can display multiple colors at once, with 100 preset lighting scenes, customizable effects, and the ability to sync to music. The lights also feature an IP67 rating for dust and water resistance.
Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium
The Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium is an excellent option for adding smarts and some style to your HVAC system. As well as being a smart way to control your energy use, the thermostat can also act as a video intercom for Ecobee’s excellent doorbell camera and an indoor air quality monitor. Read our review.
Cricut Joy 2
The Cricut Joy 2 is a small crafting machine designed for smaller projects, including custom cards, stickers, vinyl decals, labels, bookmarks, and iron-ons. It can cut designs up to 4.5 inches wide and brings Cricut’s Print Then Cut feature to its entry-level lineup. Read our review.
Amazon Echo Time
Although it’s not Amazon’s first bedside alarm clock, the Echo Time is focused on helping you sleep better. The camera-less Alexa speaker can detect your sleep stage via ultrasound and use smart alarms to ease you into the day, but only if you want it to.
The90 Gem
The90’s Gem is a UV-tracking necklace that measures UVA and UVB exposure throughout the day. articles.title: Swara Baby Products' Rs 800-cr IPO to open on Dec 2; price band fixed at Rs 105-111
articles.text:
Swara Baby Products' Rs 800-cr IPO to open on Dec 2; price band fixed at Rs 105-111
The three-day issue will close on December 4, while the bidding for anchor investors will take place on December 1, according to a public notice on Friday.
Swara Baby Products Ltd, a contract manufacturer of baby diapers, adult diapers and feminine hygiene products backed by FirstCry, will launch its Rs 800-crore initial public offering (IPO) on December 2, with a price band of Rs 105-111 per share.
The three-day issue will close on December 4, while the bidding for anchor investors will take place on December 1, according to a public notice on Friday.
At the top end of the price band, the company's market capitalisation is pegged at over Rs 3,200 crore.
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of equity shares worth Rs 500 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of shares aggregating up to Rs 300 crore.
The company proposes to utilise the net proceeds from the fresh issue to set up a new manufacturing facility in Madhya Pradesh, repay or prepay borrowings and invest in subsidiaries Solis Hygiene, Swara Hygiene and K.A. Enterprises Hygiene to repay their outstanding borrowings.
Additionally, funds will be used to pursue inorganic growth through acquisitions and for general corporate purposes.
Founded in 2018, Swara Baby manufactures disposable hygiene products across baby care, adult incontinence and feminine hygiene segments. Its portfolio includes baby diapers, adult diapers, sanitary napkins and panty liners, primarily manufactured under contract for consumer brands.
The company supplies products to customers including Brainbees Solutions, Piramal Pharma and Himalaya Wellness Company. It also markets its own brands, Cuddles and Shield, through online and modern retail channels. In December 2025, it acquired K.A. Enterprises Hygiene, a manufacturer of feminine hygiene products.
Swara Baby operates four manufacturing facilities in Pithampur and Indore, Madhya Pradesh.
For FY26, the company reported revenue from operations of Rs 1,163.9 crore, compared with Rs 942.97 crore in FY25. Profit after tax stood at Rs 95.58 crore in FY26, up from Rs 80.67 crore in the previous financial year.
The company has reserved 50 per cent of the issue for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), 15% for non-institutional investors (NIIs) and 35% for retail individual investors.
The equity shares are scheduled to list on December 9.
JM Financial and Avendus Capital are the book-running lead managers to the issue, while MUFG Intime India is the registrar.

articles.title: Victime d’une cyberattaque, l’AFP bloque une plateforme pour contrer les pirates
articles.text:
L’Agence France-Presse (AFP) a été piratée dans la nuit du mercredi 25 au jeudi 26 novembre. Vers 1 h 30 du matin, « l’AFP a été la cible d’une cyberattaque » qui « visait AFP Forum, l’une des plateformes sur lesquelles nos clients consultent et téléchargent nos contenus », explique la direction. AFP Forum sert notamment aux rédactions pour acheter les photos et les vidéos qui illustrent leurs articles.
À lire aussi : La FIFA a été piratée – des données personnelles et professionnelles ont été compromises
« Temporairement inaccessible »
Dès que l’intrusion a été détectée, les équipes techniques ont « isolé la plateforme pour la protéger ». Par mesure de précaution, la plateforme est toujours « temporairement inaccessible » ce vendredi 27 novembre 2026. Cette mesure doit empêcher les pirates de faire plus de dégâts tant que la brèche n’a pas été colmatée. Aucune date de retour n’a été communiquée pour le moment.
Sans surprise, l’AFP a promptement ouvert une enquête. L’agence de presse indique que « des analyses sont en cours, avec l’appui d’experts extérieurs ». Pour le moment, l’AFP ne dispose « d’aucun élément sur l’identité des auteurs de cette attaque » contre l’une des trois grandes agences de presse mondiales.
Pour rappel, l’agence, qui emploie 1 840 journalistes et publie en moyenne 2 300 dépêches par jour, a déjà été piratée deux ans plus tôt. En septembre 2024, l’AFP a signalé une possible fuite de données à la CNIL, le gendarme français des données personnelles.
Les fuites s’enchaînent en France
Cette nouvelle attaque s’inscrit dans le cadre d’une série noire en France. Ce mois-ci, La Poste a annoncé que sa filiale Maileva avait été piratée, et que les données de plus de 22 millions de personnes ont été dérobées. Plus récemment, c’est Decathlon, la célèbre enseigne de sport, qui s’est retrouvée dans le collimateur des pirates.
 Cybersécurité : quels sont les risques pour l’élection présidentielle en France ?
Vincent Strubel, Directeur Général de l’Anssi, est l’invité de Benjamin Duhamel et Florence Paracuellos pour la sortie de la série “Cybernation”, un podcast-fiction disponible sur l’application Radio France.
Pour en savoir plus, écoutez Le Grand entretien par Florence Paracuellos et @Ben_Duhamel ➡️ https://t.co/y13qun1Nkq
— France Inter (@franceinter) November 26, 2026
Interrogé sur France Inter avant l’attaque contre l’AFP, Vincent Strubel, le directeur général de l’Anssi, l’Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d’information, a rappelé que la France fait face à un « niveau de menace sans précédent, qui va encore augmenter ». Il ajoute que l’Hexagone « se prépare potentiellement à des chocs futurs ».

articles.title: España nunca ha tenido cuatro inviernos consecutivos sin una sola ola de frío. AEMET empieza a temer que sea algo inevitable (con todo lo que ello conlleva)
articles.text:
El día de Reyes de 2026, el termómetro de Molina de Aragón bajó hasta los 14 grados bajo cero. Era el cénit de un periodo de cinco días que dejó esa zona del país unos 5 grados por debajo de lo habitual. Dos meses después, como suele hacer, la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (AEMET) repasó el invierno y llegó a la conclusión de que, con la información disponible, nada de lo que pasó en aquellos cinco días podía considerarse una ola de frío.
No dio la talla, no entró en la lista. Lo cual tampoco es raro, porque, en fin, la lista lleva sin tener nuevos miembros desde el 2 de marzo de 2023.
Eso quiere decir que llevamos tres inviernos completos sin una sola ola de frío. Nunca en toda la serie habíamos encadenado tres. Pero eso no es lo peor: lo peor es que el cuarto empieza el 1 de diciembre.
¿Qué es una ola de frío? Es curioso. Lo primero que deja claro el estudio de referencia de AEMET es que (históricamente) no ha existido una definición oficial. También que el término se usa con "una tendencia a exagerar". Por ello, la agencia eligió un criterio a posteriori y lo aplicó, invierno a invierno, hasta 1975.
A día de hoy, una 'ola de frío' tiene que cumplir tres condiciones a la vez: a) durar al menos tres días consecutivos en el que b) como mínimo el 10% de las estaciones c) registra mínimas por debajo de un umbral.
Como tenemos apenas 131 estaciones, repartidas por la Península y Baleares (Canarias queda fuera por lo suave de sus temperaturas), hacen falta 14.
¿Y el umbral? Funciona parecido a como en las olas de calor: AEMET toma las mínimas de todos los eneros y febreros de 1971 a 2000, que suman 1778 días, y se queda con el 5% más frío: 89 noches. La más suave de ellas marca el umbral.
Vale, ya lo tenemos. De hecho, tenemos 67 olas en total: 334 días repartidos en 49 inviernos. Por lógica, ha habido inviernos en blanco (14) e incluso hay parejas de inviernos sin olas (6). Nunca hemos tenido una racha de tres ni, por supuesto, una de cuatro. Hasta ahora.
¿Y cómo lo sabes? Hay pistas. La predicción estacional de AEMET para diciembre, enero y febrero da una probabilidad muy alta de que el trimestre sea más cálido de lo normal en toda España. Copernicus apunta en la misma dirección para el suroeste de Europa. Y en el Pacífico, el último boletín de la NOAA (la agencia oceánica y atmosférica de EE. UU.) sitúa El Niño en +2,5 °C de anomalía en la región Niño 3.4; y Meteored, que planteó esta semana la posibilidad de un cuarto invierno sin olas, prevé un diciembre entre 1 y 2 °C por encima de lo normal. Pistas.
Y lo más preocupante es que no sabemos qué consecuencias va a tener.
Imagen | Shawn Dearn

articles.title: US Air Force cloud platform reportedly hacked in latest federal breach
articles.text:
Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One computing platform, adding to a recent wave of cyberattacks affecting US government agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and Treasury Department.
According to Reuters, the intrusion was discovered within the past month during an upgrade of the cloud platform, disrupting application migrations and software updates.
Launched in 2017, Cloud One is an enterprise cloud computing platform managed by the US Air Force that allows Department of Defense agencies to host and manage applications supporting military operations, personnel management, logistics, and maintenance.
According to one source who spoke to Reuters, the hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability to gain access to the platform, potentially exposing sensitive military operational and logistics information.
US Cyber Command has reportedly been called in to assess the impact, with the attackers, scope of the attack, and whether any data was stolen currently unknown.
The Air Force declined to comment on the security or operational status of the affected systems, telling Reuters that it continuously takes measures to protect its information, systems, and mission capabilities.
The reported Air Force breach follows other cybersecurity incidents disclosed over the past week targeting US federal agencies.
On November 21, it was revealed that hackers reportedly breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies.
The database contains information on wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, and other criminal justice records.
The intrusion came two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group breached FBI systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability in the agency's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov.
Earlier this week, hackers also reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The incident also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA).
Hours after the CIA breach was reported, the US Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to its systems.
It is unclear whether any of the recently disclosed federal government breaches are connected.
AI-powered hacking tools fuel cyberattacks
The CIA breach was reportedly conducted using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing platform, which the FBI recently warned was being used to automate cyberattacks worldwide.
In an advisory, the FBI said multiple threat actors had used ARTEX since at least August 2026 in attacks targeting government, defense, healthcare, financial, and technology organizations.
ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that uses AI agents to automate various stages of a cyberattack, including discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, escalating privileges, and stealing data.
The framework integrates with external AI models from Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, Grok, and others, allowing attackers to conduct autonomous attacks against organizations with minimal human intervention.
According to the FBI, some ARTEX-powered intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.
The platform was used by a Chinese state-aligned threat actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0940 in an October attack targeting ConnectWise's Cloud Backup service. Cybersecurity firm Huntress identified at least 162 compromised Microsoft 365 customer tenants during the campaign.
Other attacks linked to ARTEX include:
- Attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed personal information of approximately 67,000 people.
- A South Korean hacking campaign targeting more than 90 organizations, resulting in the theft of approximately 8.2 million data records and the arrest of seven suspects.
- A cyberespionage campaign attributed by CrowdStrike to a Chinese hacking group tracked as Vapor Panda, which targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries and compromised at least nine.
As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX management consoles, with the number believed to be much higher.
It remains unknown whether ARTEX or other AI-powered hacking tools were used in the attacks against the Air Force, FBI, or FinCEN.

articles.title: Data park project draws $50m investor push from Nigeria, Togo
articles.text:
Nigeria and Togo are seeking private investors to finance the first phase of a joint data park project estimated to cost between $30 million and $50 million to boost data centre capacity in West Africa.
The countries have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to develop what they describe as a “twin data park,” with one facility in each country operating as part of a shared project. Nigeria’s Communications Minister, Bosun Tijani, and Togo’s Digital Economy Minister, Cina Lawson, announced the agreement at a joint media briefing in Lagos on Thursday, November 26.
The plan comes as Nigeria struggles to expand data centre capacity to meet growing demand. Its commercial data centres have only about 50 to 56 megawatts of live capacity, according to research by TC Insights, a limited base for a country of more than 200 million people.
The proposed Nigerian site would sit beside the Egbin Power Plant, Nigeria’s largest thermal power station, giving operators access to power, water and connectivity difficult to secure across scattered data centre locations in Lagos.
Both governments will hold minority stakes in the project, while private investors are expected to provide most of the money. However, they have not yet named the investors or confirmed the funding sources.
“It’s going to be the first time that we do a project together with Nigeria in the digital space,” Lawson said. “It shows that Africa is changing.”
A data park is a site prepared for companies that run data centres. “We’re not building data centers; we’re building parks so that data center operators can come,” Tijani said.
Tijani said Egbin Power Station meets four needs: power for round-the-clock operation, water for cooling equipment, strong connectivity (fibre now and a possible subsea cable link later), and security.
Togo’s site has similar features, Lawson said. It is close to water and has fibre connections. The ministers did not name the Togolese data park site at the briefing.
According to an official briefing note, the Togo data park would also serve as a separate location for backup, disaster recovery and regional services. That arrangement is meant to keep services running if one site has a problem.
The ministers said the cost of the first phase has yet to be finalised. According to Tijani, transaction advisers are developing the financing plan, while discussions with the World Bank have focused on the project’s feasibility, structure and funding options.
The plan is to set up one company to own and manage both data parks, with the two governments and private investors holding stakes in it. Tijani said government should not be the biggest shareholder. He pointed to Nigeria’s liquefied natural gas projects, where government owns between 25% and 49% and private investors hold the rest, as the model.
“So, government won’t be funding this fully,” he said. “Government will see it through. Government will back it with appropriate laws. Government will make it attractive, not just in the immediate term but in the long term. In doing that, government will be able to encourage investors to come in.”
Regional data park
Lawson said the partnership helps Togo because large data-centre operators often prefer bigger countries.
“Small countries are less attractive when it comes to data centers,” she said. She said linking with Nigeria should make Togo more appealing to them.
Nigeria gains by serving the wider region, Tijani said. Togo is French-speaking and Nigeria is English-speaking, and the ministers want to attract customers from both groups across West Africa.
“I think this partnership ensures that the SPV can serve both the anglophone and francophone countries of West Africa,” he said.
Lawson said the project is open to other West African countries. “This is a regional play,” she said. She added that Togo is considering future AI data centres, though nothing has been agreed.
Tijani said the park’s success depends on laws that make operators comfortable, not only on investment. He pointed to Nigeria’s cloud policy released in August, as the country aims to attract $750 million in cloud investment.
“We can build a data park, but if we can’t attract data centers that can be profitable because of laws, it will affect the future of the data park,” he said.
Tijani also described a “data embassy” proposal, which officials are pushing through the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Modelled on the legal protection embassies receive under the Vienna Convention, it would let a country store sensitive data in another country’s park and have it treated as its own territory. Lawson said a country’s data centre on the park site would be treated as that country’s land. The rules have not yet been written.
The minister added that Nigeria already has a strong data protection law and a regulator responsible for enforcing it. He added that data belonging to foreign users would be protected under the proposed data embassy arrangement, although how that would work in practice remains to be determined.
Tijani said he wants “some elements” of the project to take shape in the second quarter of next year.
“Our wish is that Q2 next year, something is achieved,” he said, adding that raising money is not entirely within the government’s control. “If it’s not working out, we also communicate that appropriately,” he said.

articles.title: Q&A: AI Minister Evan Solomon on why Canadians won’t know the terms of the feds’ $1.6-billion Cohere investment
articles.text:
Earlier this year, AI Minister Evan Solomon revealed Canada’s refreshed AI strategy, promising the Canadian tech ecosystem a path to capital, compute, and customers, and that the government would shift from a startup supporter to a stakeholder. Over the past month, those promises have begun to move forward.
The Government of Canada revealed a QSBS-style tax incentive and sovereign compute commitments in the federal budget, and it took a hefty, $1.6-billion stake in Toronto-based frontier AI developer Cohere. Solomon has been busy.
It’s one thing to read a line item; it’s another to hear it from the man himself. Solomon joined The BetaKit Podcast to debrief on Budget 2026, pitch his plan to keep more technology companies in Canada, and explain why Canadian taxpayers shouldn’t expect to learn more details about that big Cohere investment.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Building sovereign capabilities has been a large part of your portfolio. Since we last sat down, Taalas got acquired by US chip giant AMD, and Canadian-founded, US-based Tenstorrent has reportedly lobbied Canada for sovereign AI contracts. Are you comfortable with that dynamic?
Strategically, we’ve made a very big effort to make sure that talent stays here.
If a company is still invested in Canada, and they’re hiring in Canada, and they do business in Canada, that’s great. But the problem that we’ve talked about is that we plant the seed here, we fertilize it, we grow the plant, and someone else harvests it and we lose the IP and the company headquarters. We’re trying to stop that; this is part of the budget.
We’ve got to make this the best place to invest because we want capital to come here. The Productivity Mega Deduction means that the marginal effective tax rate that a business pays here is 6.4 percent. This is by far the most effective and the lowest marginal effective tax rate. The Canada Growth Incentive is also very important. If you’ve invested in a company that’s become successful and you have an exit, you reinvest up to $15 million back into another Canadian company, then you don’t pay capital gains tax because you’ve reinvested it. This is really the engine to spin the flywheel of investment.
What I’m hearing from you is, directionally, you’re okay with Tenstorrent being on both sides of the border, but you don’t want Canadian companies having to make that choice to begin with.
Tenstorrent made that decision a couple of years ago.
When the next company is looking at the environment and, for whatever reason, they decide to redomicile, my job is to make that decision significantly more difficult because they should be able to say now, “Why? We don’t need to redomicile for access to capital. This is the best place we can get the capital. This is the best place to build a business, and we can grow around the world and stay here in Canada,” and this is the environment that I think we’ve created.
The budget also pledged 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute to Canadian companies through “backstops and offtake agreements.” Can you explain how that will work?
So here’s the problem: Compute is essentially the fuel of innovation, and it’s expensive. For small-to-medium-sized companies that are trying to buy compute, it’s really hard to get, partly because big companies buy up all the compute in these big projects and there’s not a lot left over.
Through an offtake, we can become the customer, and then we can sort of say, “Oh, you can sell the compute to us.”
You resell it to Canadian companies.
Yes. Or we can do the backstop that we actually, through financial instruments, backstop the building of compute capacity. We haven’t decided on the exact instruments. What we’re making sure of is that if there’s this race to get compute, it’s not just the big hyperscalers that can take the compute and grab it.
Let’s talk about the federal government’s $1.6-billion investment in Cohere. Why is the government choosing this approach?
Simply put, Canada’s not going to wait for others to build the AI. Maybe they would be people we don’t know or don’t trust. We’re going to build it now. Plan A is to build; that’s what every element of our strategy is.
Canada decided to take an equity stake in a strategically important company, Cohere, for three reasons. One, because we want to make sure this company stays Canadian, it’s headquartered in Canada, and its intellectual property stays in Canada. Two, Canadians should have a chance to benefit from this technology, so Canadians get an opportunity to share in the upside of this technology. And three, this gives us a seat at the table. Cohere, after it merged with Aleph Alpha, is now the largest AI language company outside the US and China. This is absolutely critical; this allows us to build in Canada according to our values and our rules.
This is a unique moment where the Canadian public now has skin in the game with a private company. How much should Canadians expect to know about the terms of this deal?
It’s an absolutely vital question. Look, we’re trying to get the best possible terms for Canadians. Our job is to make sure that Canadians benefit from this, Canadians see the upside in this, that our sovereignty and security is protected, and that we’re investing responsibly. We invest through the Canada Development Investment Corporation; they do these kinds of investments, so there’s a due diligence process.
One of the reasons why the details on the commercial terms are not released is that they’re commercially sensitive, but we are making other investments, and it is strategically important not to give away our positions because we’re trying to always negotiate the best terms for Canadians in this deal and in other deals. So again, I think Canadians will appreciate that there’s a diligence process that goes on, but we also can’t weaken our negotiating position on this and other potential investments. We’re following pretty normal investor confidence terms.

articles.title: Samsung One UI 9.5 : la liste des smartphones Galaxy qui devraient recevoir la mise à jour
Denis Villeneuve, decepcionado por estrenar ‘Dune 3’ el mismo día que ‘Avengers: Doomsday’: «Ojalá sobrevivamos»
articles.text:
El próximo 18 de diciembre se estrena Avengers: Doomsday, que apunta a ser el evento cinematográfico del año. Sin embargo, en esa misma fecha llegará a los cines de todo el mundo otro peso pesado: Dune 3. Esta es una gran noticia para los fanáticos del séptimo arte, aunque no tanto para Denis Villeneuve.
El director de Dune 3 no ocultó su fastidio por tener que compartir fecha de lanzamiento con Avengers: Doomsday. El cineasta canadiense fue bastante expresivo respecto de lo que supone salir a competir con una propuesta tan titánica como la de Marvel Studios. "Ojalá sobrevivamos", remarcó.
Villeneuve explicó que con Dune 3 apuntaba a tener un estreno más tranquilo, considerando que las dos primeras entregas de la saga llegaron a la cartelera en momentos bastante tumultuosos. Sin embargo, el retraso de Avengers: Doomsday, que originalmente iba a llegar en mayo de este año, alteró ese plan.
"Seré sincero. La primera Dune se estrenó al final de la pandemia. Logramos una gran recaudación en un contexto muy complicado, pero tuvimos todo en contra. Con la segunda película ocurrió lo mismo: debíamos estrenarla en otoño, pero tuvimos que hacerlo a finales del invierno por las dos huelgas de Hollywood. Tuvimos éxito, pero no fue fácil. Por fin, ya no hay pandemia ni huelgas a la vista. Pensé que tendríamos un estreno normal, pero Disney nos puso enfrente la franquicia más grande de todos los tiempos. No soy tonto: esas películas son un auténtico coloso", explicó el responsable de la saga Dune y director de la próxima entrega de James Bond.
El director de Dune 3, decepcionado por estrenar el mismo día que Avengers: Doomsday
Si bien Denis Villeneuve se mostró confiado con tener gran éxito de la mano de Dune 3, no ocultó su desazón tras conocer que Avengers: Doomsday llegaría a los cines el mismo fin de semana. "Me sentí profundamente decepcionado. Pero nos habíamos comprometido con esta fecha, con IMAX. Era imposible cambiarla. Así que acepté mi destino, rezando a los dioses del cine. Dune no es un coloso como Avengers, pero es una criatura atractiva que cuenta con mucho poder de fuego. Ojalá sobrevivamos", comentó.
Recordemos que, en un principio, Marvel Studios iba a lanzar Avengers: Doomsday el 1 de mayo de 2026 y Avengers: Secret Wars el 7 de mayo de 2027. Sin embargo, a mediados del año pasado Disney anunció que retrasaría ambas películas hasta el 18 de diciembre de 2026 y el 17 de diciembre de 2027, respectivamente.
La tercera entrega de Dune ya tenía estipulada la fecha de finales de 2026, así que no había posibilidades de cambiarla. Ahora, los fanáticos esperan que las dos cintas repitan el fenómeno que se dio hace algunos años con Barbie y Oppenheimer. "Podría ser uno de los fines de semana de mayor taquilla de todos los tiempos, gracias a ambas películas. ¿Estoy compitiendo contra Avengers? En absoluto. Es un Tiranosaurio rex. Pero me siento orgulloso, porque creo que la película cumple", reflexionó sobre las posibilidades de Dune 3.

articles.title: Inoffizieller „GTA 6“-Port für den PC: Soweit sind Bastler schon
articles.text:
GTA 6 läuft bereits auf dem PC – aber Rockstar hat damit nichts zu tun
Eine inoffizielle PC-Version von GTA 6 rückt näher: Neue Videos zeigen einzelne Szenen des Spiels auf Windows-Rechnern mit mehr als 30 Bildern pro Sekunde. Vollständig spielbar ist der Toptitel, der derzeit nur für Xbox und Playstation 5 erhältlich ist, auf dem PC aber weiterhin nicht.
Wie der Trick funktioniert
Die meisten Fortschritte bauen auf „VIctory“ auf. Diese quelloffene Kompatibilitätsschicht führt den Code der Xbox-Version direkt unter Windows aus. Die Spieldateien müssen Nutzer selbst mitbringen – einen legalen Weg dafür gibt es bisher nicht. Stattdessen greifen viele auf die von Hacker „Cyberleek“ geleakte Xbox-Version zurück. Dieser hatte auch eine .exe-Datei verbreitet, die den Start erst möglich macht.
In sozialen Medien kursieren zahlreiche Clips verschiedener Portierungen, die Ausschnitte mit über 30 Bildern pro Sekunde zeigen. An der Stabilität hapert es noch. Dass einzelne Szenen flüssig laufen, heißt aber nicht, dass das ganze Spiel funktioniert. Einzelne Videos lassen sich zudem kaum überprüfen.
Ein Wettrennen der Modder
Die Community behandelt die Portierung wie einen „Speedrun“: Der Fortschritt der einzelnen Projekte wird wie bei einem Wettrennen verfolgt. Laut der Webseite PortWatch führt derzeit der Modder Belobug die Rangliste an, dessen Version als „spielbar“ gilt. Auf einer Radeon RX 9070 XT erreicht sie PortWatch zufolge im Schnitt aber nur rund 22 Bilder pro Sekunde, ohne abzustürzen. Mehrere andere Projekte sind dicht dahinter.
Die Ports unterscheiden sich in Bildqualität, Stabilität und unterstützter Hardware. Bei allen bekannten Versionen treten noch Bildfehler und ein ungleichmäßiger Bildfluss auf. Auch das Raytracing der Konsolenfassungen, also die realistische Licht- und Schattenberechnung, arbeitet nicht korrekt. Von einer fertigen PC-Version kann deshalb keine Rede sein. Mit Hilfe von KI kommen die Modder aber täglich ein gutes Stück weiter.
Take-Two geht gegen die Projekte vor
Der Publisher Take-Two versucht unterdessen, die Entwicklung zu stoppen. Vor einigen Tagen ließ er das Rekompilierungsprojekt Leonida von GitHub entfernen. Gesperrt wurden neben dem Haupt-Repository auch sämtliche Kopien, insgesamt 3007 Repositories.
In seinem Antrag nach dem US-Urheberrecht (DMCA) argumentiert Take-Two, das Projekt sei ein abgeleitetes Werk von GTA 6 und verstoße gegen Rockstars Nutzungsbedingungen. Diese verbieten es, die Software zu analysieren und nachzubauen. Dass Leonida selbst keine Spieldateien enthielt, ließ der Publisher nicht gelten. Abgesehen vom Leak kommen Käufer der Xbox-Version ohnehin nicht direkt an lesbare Spieldateien: Installierte Xbox-Spiele bleiben verschlüsselt. Das Spiel war in diesem Monat für Konsolen erschienen. Mit einer offiziellen PC-Version wird nicht vor dem kommenden Jahr gerechnet. Sie ist nicht einmal angekündigt.

articles.title: Our 2027 Innovators Under 35 competition is now open
articles.text:
Our 2027 Innovators Under 35 competition is now open
Nominate yourself or someone you know by January 19.
Every year, the editors at MIT Technology Review select 35 of the world’s top young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors to honor as our newest class of Innovators Under 35. And starting today, our 2027 competition is officially open for nominations.
We’re on the hunt for researchers and founders who are engineering solutions to some of the most formidable problems society faces, including human disease and climate change. We also recognize those who have made clever and useful inventions, important new scientific discoveries, or technological breakthroughs early in their careers.
We want to hear about people, based anywhere in the world, who are responsible for a major finding or advance and can show real-world impact from their work. To qualify for the list, a nominee must be under the age of 35 as of October 1, 2027 (that is, born on or after October 2, 1992).
Have someone in mind? Or think you’d be a great candidate and want to nominate yourself? Follow this link to suggest someone who you think should make our 2027 list. It’s free and takes only a few minutes. Just be sure to get your nomination in before the deadline—which is 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, January 19.
After the deadline, our editors will review all nominees and select a group of semifinalists, whom we’ll invite to complete a formal application. Then, dozens of expert judges will help us evaluate those applicants and settle on the finalists. You can read more about our selection process here.
Our newsroom began producing our Innovators Under 35 list in 1999. It’s an annual exercise that helps our reporters scout out the brightest young minds in the fields they cover. It also introduces our audience to dozens of rising stars worth watching in the years to come. Subscribers can explore the 2026 list and peruse the full archives.
We look forward to reviewing your nominations.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
  November 17, 2026
- Source:
  University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
  A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
