articles.title: The best Black Friday deals you can still get on AirPods, Macs, and other Apple gear
articles.text:
Black Friday is entering the evening, which means one of the best times of the year to save some cash on a new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch is coming to a close. After all, the holiday savings can help offset the unfortunate price hikes from earlier this year, when Apple raised the cost of some of its most popular gear. Some discounts still apply to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro, too, which are available at their lowest prices to date.
The best Black Friday deals you can still get on AirPods, Macs, and other Apple gear
We dug up the biggest price drops on Apple hardware and accessories before Black Friday officially ends.
In addition to a variety of discounts across retailers, Apple is offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases between November 27th and November 30th. How much you get back is determined by how much you spend, with up to $100 available for some iPhone and Apple Watch purchases, and up to $300 for the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That said, in some cases you may be able to save more by buying from other retailers.
Earbud and headphone deals
AirPods Pro 3
The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review.
Beats Powerbeats Pro 2
Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review.
- You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review.
- The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Target also has them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review.
Beats Studio Pro
The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review.
Beats 360 headphones
The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.
- If you want over-ears and are comfortable going without active noise cancellation, the Beats Solo 4 are on sale starting at $79.99 ($120 off) at Amazon and Target — a new low price. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. They also last up to 50 hours on a single charge, while their memory foam ear cushions make them comfortable enough for long listening sessions. Read our review.
- The Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target, nearly matching their lowest price to date. The wireless earbuds feature a slick, eye-catching transparent option and solid noise cancellation, especially at this price. They’re also exceptionally comfortable, with four ear tip sizes to help you find a secure fit. Sure, you don’t get wireless charging, but they offer IPX4 water resistance and up to nine hours of battery life on a single charge. Read our review.
MacBook deals
MacBook Neo
Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5)
Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.
- The recently released 16.3-inch MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage is on sale starting at $3,099 ($300 off) — a new low price — at Amazon. The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. It’s also noticeably thinner and lighter than the non-touchscreen 16-inch MacBook Pro, and features a new Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and provides quick access to controls and notifications. Read our review.
- The 14-inch M6-powered MacBook Pro is on sale starting at $1,749 ($250 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is a new low price. The Pro builds on its predecessor with a faster chip and support for Wi-Fi 7. In our testing, it handled multitasking, photo editing, and occasional video editing with ease while still delivering exceptional battery life. It lacks the newer MacBook Pro’s gorgeous OLED display, but its Mini LED screen still looks great, especially given its smooth 120Hz refresh rate. It also offers excellent speakers and a good selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SD card slot. Read our review.
Apple Watch deals
Apple Watch Series 12
The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.
- The Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration starting at $179 ($50 off) at Amazon and Walmart, matching its best price to date, while Best Buy is currently $20 higher. Apple’s newest entry-level smartwatch remains our top recommendation for anyone who wants a basic fitness tracker, as it offers all the essentials alongside an always-on display and Apple’s S10 chip, which enables on-device Siri requests. Read our review.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.
Baseus AM52 power bank (with built-in cable)
The Baseus PicoGo AM52 is a 10,000mAh magnetic power bank that supports fast 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging and up to 45W wired charging via its built-in USB-C cable. It was one of the fastest wireless chargers we tested, bringing an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 65 percent in an hour. Read our guide to the best Qi2 batteries.
Apple iPad (11th-gen)
Apple’s 11th-gen iPad offers 128GB of storage — twice that of its predecessor — and runs on a faster A16 chip. It also comes in four colors: blue, pink, yellow, and silver.
- You can buy the last-gen iPad Mini with 128GB of storage and Wi-Fi on Amazon in select colors for $484 ($115 off), which is the best price we’ve seen since Apple’s recent price hikes. It has a smaller screen and a slower chip than the newer model, and it lacks an OLED screen, the Acoustic Display, and water resistance. Still, it’s a great option for reading and everyday use that’s currently more affordable than its $599 successor, with support for Apple Intelligence and the Apple Pencil Pro. Read our review.
- Apple’s latest Magic Mouse is matching its all-time low of $59.99 ($20 off) at Amazon. The wireless mouse features a touch-sensitive surface that lets you scroll through documents and swipe between apps with simple gestures; it also pairs automatically with compatible Macs and offers support for USB-C.
Apple Pencil (USB-C)
Apple’s entry-level stylus attaches magnetically to supported iPads, though it doesn’t support magnetic charging. Instead, you pair and charge it by connecting it to your device’s USB-C port. It includes tilt sensitivity and Apple Pencil Hover support, but it doesn’t offer double-tap gestures or pressure sensitivity.
Sharge Icemag 3 Power Bank
The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.
Apple Studio Display (2026)
Designed to pair with a Mac, the latest Apple Studio Display features a sharp 5K Retina display, a great 12-megapixel Center Stage camera that keeps you in frame during video calls, and a good six-speaker sound system with spatial audio. Sadly, it only offers two Thunderbolt 5 ports in addition to a pair of USB-C ports. Read our review.
Update, November 27th: Updated to reflect current pricing / availability and a newer deal on the Apple Pencil (USB-C).

articles.title: ChatGPT: Neue Regeln für Nutzungslimits ab Dezember
articles.text:
Bislang waren der Chat und OpenAIs Work-Angebot zwei separate Elemente in der ChatGPT-App für den Desktop. Das will das Unternehmen jetzt sukzessive ändern. Beide Teile sollen in einer gemeinsamen Oberfläche zusammenfließen. Ausprobieren darf das vorerst nur eine kleine Gruppe von Pro-Nutzer:innen, wie Product Lead Thibault Sottiaux auf X mitteilt. Demnach wolle man zunächst Feedback von dieser kleinen Gruppe einholen, bevor man die Zusammenlegung breiter verfügbar macht.
OpenAI kombiniert Nutzungslimits
Bei der Kombination aus Chat- und Work-Oberfläche allein wird es aber nicht bleiben. Laut Techcrunch wird OpenAI zudem die Nutzungslimits für beide Elemente sowie für Codex für Abonnent:innen der Plus-, Pro und Business-Pläne kombinieren. Das geht auf einen Sprecher des Unternehmens zurück. Nutzer:innen in den sozialen Medien befürchten schon jetzt, dass sie dadurch ihr Nutzungslimit deutlich schneller erreichen werden und ChatGPT nicht mehr in gewohnter Form nutzen können. Außerdem zahlen sie trotz Zusammenlegung weiterhin dieselben Preise.
Der namentlich nicht genannte Sprecher versucht, gegenüber Techcrunch zu beschwichtigen. So sollen die allermeisten Nutzer:innen von der Neuregelung nichts spüren. Lediglich einige wenige Heavy-User könnten ihr Limit künftig schneller als gewohnt erreichen.
Ausgeschlossen von dem Nutzungslimit ist der sogenannte Instant-Chat, also die Einstellung für alltägliche Fragen und schnelle Antworten. Sie lässt sich weiter nutzen, auch nachdem das Nutzungslimit für Work oder größere Modelle für komplexe Anfragen aufgebraucht ist. OpenAI wolle zudem an der Effizienz von ChatGPT arbeiten, sodass zahlende Kund:innen mehr aus ihrem Abo herausholen könnten.
Unbekannt bleibt zunächst, wann genau das Unternehmen die kombinierte Oberfläche für weitere Kund:innen zugänglich machen will. Die gemeinsamen Nutzungslimits sollen aber ab Dezember für alle Kund:innen gelten.

articles.title: Millonarios vs. Bucaramanga ver en Roja Directa, Xuper Tv o Fútbol Libre: el truco gratuito que vació cuentas
articles.text:
Buscar Millonarios contra Bucaramanga en Roja Directa, Xuper TV o Fútbol Libre puede parecer una salida rápida para seguir el duelo, pero esos accesos gratuitos pueden ocultar un fraude capaz de vaciar cuentas y comprometer dispositivos.
El partido que se disputó en Bogotá, por la segunda fecha de los cuadrangulares semifinales de la Liga BetPlay 2026-2, impulsó búsquedas de señales sin pago.
El problema trasciende los cortes de imagen o la publicidad invasiva. Páginas sin autorización y aplicaciones distribuidas fuera de canales oficiales utilizan reproductores falsos, formularios, redirecciones y descargas para captar contraseñas, datos bancarios o archivos personales. ESET ha advertido sobre la relación entre el streaming no oficial y el software malicioso; Interpol alerta sobre virus y estafas financieras.
Dónde ver Millonarios vs. Bucaramanga de manera segura
Millonarios y Atlético Bucaramanga abrirán la jornada en el estadio Nemesio Camacho El Campín de Bogotá, desde las 18:20. El conjunto dirigido por Alberto Gamero igualó sin goles ante Deportivo Cali, mientras que el equipo de Pablo Peirano firmó un 2-2 contra América de Cali. La señal autorizada estará disponible por Win Play y Win+ Fútbol.
Los cuatro clubes tienen un punto, por lo que una nueva igualdad puede dificultar la clasificación, sobre todo porque América de Cali cuenta con ventaja deportiva. El contexto explica el interés por encontrar emisiones gratuitas.
Por qué aparece publicidad en las páginas piratas
En los portales piratas es frecuente encontrar botones repetidos con iconos de reproducción. Algunos llevan a anuncios, extensiones del navegador o archivos de instalación, en vez de abrir la transmisión. También pueden ofrecer una actualización urgente o un programa adicional como condición para ver el fútbol. En teléfonos, computadoras y televisores inteligentes, esas descargas pueden instalar programas espía, troyanos o publicidad persistente.
Android, Apple, Microsoft y los fabricantes de televisores aplican controles a sus catálogos. Los archivos obtenidos en dominios desconocidos no ofrecen esas garantías. Una aplicación ilegal puede modificar ajustes, incorporar programas adicionales y permanecer activa después del encuentro. Por eso, cualquier solicitud para instalar un archivo externo debe considerarse una señal de alerta.
Cómo roban datos Roja Directa, Fútbol Libre o Xuper TV
Antes de mostrar una señal, una web puede pedir una verificación de edad, un registro o una activación de cuenta. En ese proceso, el visitante puede entregar correo electrónico, teléfono, contraseña o datos de tarjeta sin saber quién administra la página.
El engaño gana eficacia cuando copia el diseño de un servicio conocido o emplea mensajes de urgencia. Un pago pequeño para desbloquear el contenido también debe despertar sospechas.
Una clave robada puede permitir acceso al correo, redes sociales y aplicaciones de mensajería, especialmente si se reutiliza en varios servicios. Los permisos para leer archivos, revisar aplicaciones activas, usar el micrófono, enviar notificaciones o instalar programas merecen atención.
No resultan necesarios para una reproducción básica. Si una aplicación descargada desde una fuente desconocida incorpora código malicioso, puede afectar fotografías, documentos, grabaciones y otros equipos conectados a la misma red doméstica.
Las direcciones que cambian con frecuencia, los errores de redacción, las alertas falsas de virus y la publicidad que promete premios son indicios para cerrar la página. Los servidores proxy tampoco aseguran privacidad: un operador poco fiable puede registrar la navegación o incorporar nuevas amenazas.
Las retransmisiones deportivas están protegidas por derechos audiovisuales, y quienes administran, monetizan o redistribuyen señales no autorizadas afrontan mayor exposición legal.
Para evitar la entrega de datos y las descargas ocultas, conviene consultar los canales oficiales de la competición, los clubes y los operadores con licencia. En este caso, Win+ Fútbol y Win Play son las opciones informadas para seguir el partido. La gratuidad aparente de Roja Directa, Xuper TV o Fútbol Libre puede tener un costo mayor si termina en una cuenta bancaria comprometida o un dispositivo infectado.

articles.title: Microsoft removes WSUS server role in Windows Server 2028
articles.text:
Microsoft will remove the WSUS server role from Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system.
Introduced in 2005 as Software Update Services (SUS), WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) lets IT administrators manage and distribute updates for Microsoft products across corporate networks with many Windows devices.
It gives admins centralized control over the updates, rather than having each device download them individually from Microsoft's servers.
Microsoft has officially deprecated WSUS in September 2024, but said that it still plans to maintain functionality and continue publishing updates through the channel. The change affects enterprise environments that rely on WSUS to manage updates delivered to many devices but does not impact home users or those using Microsoft Configuration Manager.
In a recently updated support document, Microsoft went even further and confirmed that Windows Server 2028 removes the WSUS server role altogether.
"WSUS remains available and supported in earlier Windows Server releases, including Windows Server 2025, for the duration of each release's support lifecycle. You can continue to use WSUS on those releases to manage updates for supported Windows client and Windows Server releases, which includes updates to Windows Server 2028," it said.
"Microsoft recognizes the need to manage updates in disconnected and highly controlled environments. We're invested in supporting these scenarios and we'll share more as the work progresses."
Businesses are now encouraged to adopt cloud-based solutions, such as Windows Autopatch, Microsoft Intune, and Azure Update Manager, for keeping endpoints and servers on their network up to date.
"While the WSUS role remains available in Windows Server 2025, we recommend organizations transition to cloud tools, including including Windows Autopatch and Microsoft Intune for client update management and Azure Update Manager for server update management," Microsoft's Nir Froimovici said in September 2024. "Remember: WSUS remains operational but is no longer investing in new features."
Windows Server 2028 also removes VBScript (disabled by default in Internet Explorer 11 on Windows 10) and the legacy Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line (WMIC) utility (deprecated in Windows Server 2012 and Windows 10 21H1) to thwart a wide range of malware and attack tactics abusing them.
Windows Internet Name Service (WINS) support, deprecated with the release of Windows Server 2022 in August 2021, is also being removed in the next Windows Server version, as Microsoft announced a year ago.
Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028 last week at the Ignite 2026 conference, and it can be tested by registering for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or applying to enroll in the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP) for earlier access.

articles.title: El SEPE concederá a partir de 2027 el subsidio por desempleo a los trabajadores si acreditan rentas inferiores a 964 euros brutos mensuales
articles.text:
Si estás cobrando un subsidio por desempleo o tienes pensado solicitarlo el próximo año, hay un cambio que te interesa conocer. El Gobierno aprobó el 17 de noviembre la subida del Salario Mínimo Interprofesional (SMI) hasta los 1.286 euros mensuales en 14 pagas, un 5,3% más que en 2026. Y aunque pueda parecer que esta medida solo afecta a los salarios, también modificará las condiciones económicas para acceder a las ayudas del SEPE.
El motivo es bastante sencillo: para cobrar la mayoría de los subsidios por desempleo sujetos a un límite de rentas, tus ingresos no pueden superar el 75% del salario mínimo, sin contar las pagas extraordinarias del SMI. Hasta ahora ese máximo estaba en 915,75 euros mensuales, pero desde el 1 de enero de 2027 subirá casi 50 euros.
Qué ingresos tendrá en cuenta el SEPE desde enero
Con el nuevo salario mínimo, el límite quedará fijado en 964,50 euros al mes, tal y como explica elEconomista en su información sobre el cambio. Esto significa que algunas personas que actualmente superan el máximo permitido podrían cumplir el requisito económico el próximo año, siempre que reúnan las demás condiciones de la ayuda.
Eso sí, el SEPE no se fija únicamente en tu nómina. También cuenta los ingresos procedentes de alquileres, intereses bancarios, pensiones y determinadas ganancias patrimoniales. El artículo 275 de la Ley General de la Seguridad Social establece que se revisan las rentas del mes natural anterior a la solicitud, prórroga o reanudación del subsidio.
Hay algo más que conviene tener claro: este aumento no significa que vayas a cobrar 964,50 euros de subsidio. Esa cifra es el máximo de rentas permitido para cumplir el requisito económico, no el importe de la prestación. Y encontrarse por debajo del límite tampoco garantiza que el SEPE conceda la ayuda, porque cada subsidio mantiene sus propios requisitos.

articles.title: Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Smartphone GPS, motion sensors, and vehicle interfaces can each report valid measurements that produce incorrect results when combined without accounting for timing and coordinate frames.
- Preserve raw observations and their provenance before synchronizing, transforming, or normalizing them.
- Introduce a quality gate that determines whether telemetry is suitable for a particular decision instead of forcing every observation into a definitive result.
- Design for real-world conditions, including delayed GPS updates, phone movement, background interruptions, and intermittent connectivity.
- Monitor data quality alongside conventional application and infrastructure metrics because a functioning pipeline can still produce unreliable driving events.
Why this matters: the phone is not the vehicle
A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.
Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.
However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.
In fact, a GPS update may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.
Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.
I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.
This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.
Who should read this, and what will they gain?
For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.
For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.
For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.
For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.
The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.
How this architecture took shape
I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.
This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.
Start with the architecture, not the algorithm
I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.
A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image shows. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.
Figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author)
1. Collect and preserve raw observations
Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.
A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.
Why preserve the original? Because a later transformation may be incorrect, an assumption may change, or an event may be disputed. If the system retains only its normalized output, engineers may be unable to determine whether the original observation was poor or the transformation introduced the error.
For example, suppose an application converts a GPS speed reading into a standardized unit and later combines it with vehicle speed. If an event looks implausible, the engineering team should be able to inspect the original value, its timestamp, and the conversion applied to it.
Preservation does not mean keeping every field forever, since retention, privacy, security, and storage policies still apply. It means defining which evidence is needed for diagnosis and traceability before transformations discard it.
2. Establish temporal alignment
Sensor streams do not necessarily report at the same frequency or on the same schedule. A vehicle interface may produce frequent speed updates while GPS observations arrive less often. Mobile and backend components may also introduce different buffering and delivery delays.
The first distinction I make is between measurement time and arrival time.
Measurement time describes when the observation was captured, according to its source clock. Arrival time describes when a component received it. Arrival time is useful for understanding latency, but it is not a safe substitute for measurement time when reconstructing physical events.
A stream processor that compares the latest values received from two sources can accidentally compare different moments. This becomes especially problematic during rapid acceleration, braking, or turning, when the underlying state changes quickly.
The architecture should therefore define an alignment policy. It needs to specify how observations are matched, how much temporal separation is acceptable for each use case, and what happens when the system cannot find a suitable match.
Interpolation may be appropriate for some continuous signals, but it should not be applied indiscriminately. It can create a plausible-looking value where the evidence is sparse, and it may obscure a sharp change. The system should retain whether a value was directly measured, interpolated, or otherwise estimated.
When alignment cannot be established within the required tolerance, the right result may be lower confidence or no event at all.
3. Normalize coordinate frames and measurement semantics
A measurement's value is only part of its meaning. Its unit, coordinate frame, source, and interpretation matter just as much.
A phone's accelerometer reports motion in device coordinates. Those axes are attached to the phone, not inherently to the vehicle. If the phone rotates in a mount, the relationship between the phone's axes and the vehicle's forward, lateral, and vertical directions changes.
A system that assumes the phone is always mounted in the same orientation can interpret device movement as vehicle movement. That can distort acceleration, braking, and turning estimates.
Normalization should make these assumptions explicit. It may include unit conversion, coordinate transformation, sensor calibration, and checks on the validity of orientation estimates. A transformed observation should retain enough information to identify the transformation and its assumptions.
The system must also distinguish coordinate normalization from measurement quality. A transformation can be mathematically correct but based on an uncertain orientation estimate. The result may therefore remain unsuitable for a particular event calculation.
4. Evaluate data quality before accepting a measurement
At this stage, the system asks a different question: not simply whether a value exists, but whether it is fit for the intended use.
Useful checks include freshness, timestamp alignment, missing samples, source consistency, measurement uncertainty, and the reliability of any required coordinate transformation.
These checks should not be buried inside individual event rules. A shared quality stage gives different event detectors a consistent view of the evidence and makes quality decisions easier to monitor and test.
I would use three broad outcomes:
- Accept: The observation meets the requirements for the intended calculation.
- Degrade: The observation remains useful, but the system should limit its use or communicate reduced confidence.
- Abstain: The available evidence does not support a decision that is reliable enough for the intended use.
These are not universal labels with fixed thresholds. A GPS observation might be adequate for a coarse trip map but unsuitable for calculating a short, sharp braking event. Quality must be evaluated in context.
5. Detect events using qualified evidence
Event detection should consume measurements that have already passed through the relevant quality checks.
This does not mean every event requires every sensor. A trip-start detector and a harsh-braking detector have different evidence requirements. The architecture should allow each detector to declare what it needs and how it handles missing or uncertain inputs.
Consider a braking detector that combines vehicle speed and GPS speed. If the two values refer to different moments, the detector may infer a rate of deceleration that is not supported by the underlying movement. A quality-aware design prevents the detector from treating a poor match as equivalent to aligned observations.
The detector should also distinguish the event's classification from the quality of its evidence. An event may be a candidate for further review rather than a definitive result. Keeping these concepts separate makes the system easier to tune without changing the meaning of quality checks throughout the pipeline.
6. Produce a decision with supporting evidence
The final stage produces more than an event label.
A useful event record can include the event type, event time or interval, relevant vehicle or trip association, quality status, supporting observations, and the processing-rule version. Where a confidence estimate is used, its meaning and limitations should be documented rather than treating it as a universal probability of correctness.
This information makes a decision inspectable. An engineer can trace an event to the observations that supported it, see whether any measurements were downgraded, and understand which processing logic was applied.
It also helps separate two questions that are often conflated: "What did the system decide?" and "What evidence justified that decision?"
These six stages form one continuous data path. Raw preservation protects the evidence; temporal alignment and normalization make observations comparable; the quality gate determines their suitability; event detection applies the domain logic; and the final record explains the result.
How the six stages work together
The value of this architecture comes from the boundaries between stages.
- If the phone and vehicle speed measurements disagree, temporal alignment checks whether they describe comparable moments.
- If a phone rotates, normalization identifies that the relationship between device axes and vehicle axes has changed.
- If the available evidence remains insufficient, the quality gate prevents the uncertainty from disappearing.
- The event detector uses only evidence that meets the requirements for its task.
- The final output retains enough provenance and quality information to support investigation and improvement.
This is deliberately more than a sensor-fusion algorithm. It is a contract for how imperfect physical observations become software decisions.
The principle is straightforward: preserve what was measured, establish what it means, evaluate whether it is fit for use, and only then act on it.
Real-world example 1: The phantom braking event
Imagine a fleet operator whose mobile application scores driving behavior. Drivers receive alerts for harsh braking, and fleet managers use the events to identify potentially risky patterns.
One morning, a driver approaches a traffic light and brakes normally. The smartphone collects GPS-derived speed while the vehicle interface reports speed independently. The backend later records a harsh-braking event.
The driver disputes the alert. The vehicle did slow down, but not as abruptly as the application claims.
The engineering team examines the processing flow and discovers that the phone and vehicle streams were paired by arrival order. GPS updates were less frequent, and one observation represented an earlier point in the journey. During deceleration, the system compared that older speed estimate with a more recent vehicle measurement.
The discrepancy looked like physical behavior. Part of it was actually a timing problem.
The pipeline had accepted both values because they were syntactically valid. It had no mechanism to establish whether they were temporally comparable.
Figure 2. How a timing mismatch can create a misleading event (Source: created by the author)
What changes?
The team introduces a temporal-alignment stage before event detection. Each observation retains its measurement timestamp, while arrival time is tracked separately. The pipeline evaluates the freshness of each observation and avoids comparing streams when timing uncertainty exceeds the application's defined tolerance.
The detector also stops treating every speed discrepancy as equivalent. When the measurements are not sufficiently aligned, it lowers confidence or abstains from generating a definitive event.
The team adds monitoring for timestamp offsets, stale observations, alignment failures, and event reclassification. These metrics help distinguish a change in driving behavior from a change in data quality.
This approach does not guarantee that every braking event will be classified correctly. It gives engineers a way to identify a measurement-comparison problem before treating it as driver behavior.
The same pattern applies to fleet diagnostics, trip reconstruction, usage-based insurance, and connected-vehicle analytics.
The lesson: before interpreting disagreement between sensors as physical behavior, establish whether the measurements are temporally comparable.
Coordinate frames: accurate measurements can still mean the wrong thing
Time alignment does not solve the second major problem: orientation.
An accelerometer measures along the device's axes. A vehicle-relative interpretation assumes that the system knows how those axes relate to the vehicle. If the phone rotates, that relationship changes.
The gyroscope can help estimate rotation, and sensor-fusion algorithms can estimate orientation. Neither eliminates uncertainty automatically. Estimates may drift, the initial orientation may be unknown, and the phone can move independently of the vehicle.
A field named longitudinalAcceleration can therefore be misleading if it was calculated from device-relative measurements while the phone's orientation was uncertain.
The architecture should distinguish raw device-frame measurements from transformed estimates and preserve the assumptions behind each transformation.
Real-world example 2: The phone moves, but the vehicle does not turn
Consider a mobile telematics application that detects cornering and sudden lateral movement using the phone's accelerometer and gyroscope.
A driver starts a journey with the phone secured in a horizontal dashboard mount. The application estimates orientation and interprets motion relative to the vehicle. Later, the mount loosens on a rough road, and the phone rotates. The driver continues straight.
The application detects apparent lateral movement and records an aggressive-turning event.
The sensor values changed, but the physical interpretation was wrong. The device's orientation changed, so the relationship between its axes and the vehicle's direction of travel was no longer the same.
This problem is easy to miss when testing only with a phone mounted in a fixed position. The algorithm may perform well in a controlled setup and fail when users reposition the phone, adjust the mount, or carry it during a trip.
Figure 3. The device frame is not automatically the vehicle frame (Source: created by the author)
What changes?
The team makes orientation confidence an explicit input to event detection. Raw accelerometer and gyroscope observations are preserved, while transformed measurements carry metadata describing the estimated reference frame and the confidence in that transformation.
The detector no longer assumes that one phone orientation remains valid for the entire journey. It monitors orientation changes and identifies periods when the relationship between the device and vehicle is uncertain.
When orientation is reliable, the application can use transformed measurements according to its validated detection policy. When confidence falls, it can rely on other trustworthy evidence, reduce the confidence of the event, or abstain from making a definitive classification.
The team tests deliberate phone rotations, loose mounts, different mounting positions, and periods when orientation cannot be estimated reliably. It measures false positives and false negatives against a defined reference rather than assuming that a more sophisticated algorithm automatically improves accuracy.
This also improves the user experience. Instead of penalizing a driver for an uncertain observation, the application can indicate that it could not classify the event reliably.
The lesson: sensor accuracy and interpretation accuracy are different things. A sensor can report its measurement correctly while the application assigns that measurement the wrong physical meaning.
The same principle applies to phone-based activity recognition, wearable devices, robotics, and industrial IoT.
The quality gate: a contract between sensors and business logic
The quality gate is the fourth stage in the architecture, but its responsibility extends beyond checking whether sensor values look reasonable. It determines whether the available measurements are reliable enough for the specific decision an application intends to make.
The preceding stages preserve observations, establish temporal relationships, and normalize their measurement semantics. However, even after these steps, the resulting measurements may still contain uncertainty, missing samples, or inconsistencies. Without an explicit quality evaluation, individual event detectors must handle these conditions independently, often using different assumptions and fallback rules. This can lead to inconsistent decisions across the application.
I consider the quality gate a contract between the telemetry pipeline and the business logic that consumes its output. It makes the limitations of the available evidence explicit and defines what downstream components are permitted to do with it.
This section explores three aspects of that contract: why measurement quality must be evaluated in the context of the intended decision, how the system should distinguish between accepting, degrading, and abstaining from a result, and why abstention should be treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a processing failure.
Quality depends on the decision
Suppose a fleet application supports two functions: displaying the approximate route of a trip and identifying a short, aggressive braking maneuver.
The route display may tolerate a less frequent location update. The braking detector needs evidence that is sufficiently aligned in time and suitable for estimating a rapid change in speed.
Using the same universal threshold for both functions can be unnecessarily restrictive for one and dangerously permissive for the other.
Instead, each consumer should declare its requirements. The quality gate evaluates the observation against those requirements and communicates the outcome.
This approach also makes product trade-offs explicit. If a team wants more events at the expense of accepting weaker evidence, that decision becomes a documented policy choice that can be evaluated—not an accidental consequence of a permissive fallback in a detector.
Abstention is a valid result
Engineering teams often focus on maximizing the number of events detected. But a system that always returns an answer can create a false sense of certainty.
Abstention is useful when the evidence does not support the intended decision. It should not be treated as an exception that disappears into a log file.
The system should record why it abstained, whether additional data could resolve the uncertainty, and whether the decision needs to be revisited. For some use cases, waiting briefly for a delayed observation is reasonable. For others, the system may need to return an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome.
This is especially important when events influence human decisions, scores, or downstream automation. A clearly identified lack of evidence is often more useful than a precise-looking result that cannot be defended.
Make data quality observable
A quality-aware architecture is only as good as the team's ability to see it working. If the system records only the number of events generated, it becomes difficult to distinguish a genuine change in driving behavior from a change in sensor availability, application lifecycle, or processing logic.
I would monitor the quality pipeline alongside the business outcomes.
Useful operational signals include:
- Freshness: How old are observations when a consumer uses them?
- Temporal alignment: How far apart are measurements paired for the same calculation?
- Sampling gaps: How often do expected observations go missing, and how long do gaps last?
- Quality outcomes: What proportion of observations are accepted, degraded, or rejected, and for what reasons?
- Orientation confidence: How often does an orientation-dependent calculation lack a sufficiently reliable transformation?
- Event stability: How often are candidate events revised or reclassified after delayed observations arrive?
- Processing latency: How long does it take from measurement to event decision, separately from the measurement's age?
- Provenance completeness: Can an event be traced to its supporting observations and processing-rule version?
These measurements should be segmented where useful by device type, operating-system version, sensor source, application version, and collection conditions. Otherwise, a system-wide average may conceal a failure affecting a particular group of devices.
I would also connect quality metrics to event outcomes. If the number of harsh-braking events suddenly rises, the team should be able to investigate whether driving behavior changed, timestamp skew increased, or a new application version altered sampling behavior.
This requires a distinction between technical metrics and business metrics. Event counts and driver scores tell us what the application concluded. Freshness, alignment, and rejection metrics help explain whether the evidence behind those conclusions changed.
Observability should support investigation, not just dashboards. Logs and event records need enough structured context to reconstruct a decision while respecting data-retention and privacy requirements.
Account for the mobile operating system
A smartphone sensor pipeline does not run in a perfectly controlled environment. Applications can move into the background, devices can enter power-saving modes, connectivity can disappear, and operating systems can constrain background execution.
The architecture should not assume that a requested sampling rate guarantees a continuous stream.
On the device, collection code should handle sensor unavailability, sampling gaps, lifecycle transitions, and local buffering. When connectivity returns, queued observations may arrive in a burst or out of order. The backend should therefore apply its temporal-alignment and duplicate-handling policies even when the data originated from a single phone.
The system should preserve the distinction between the time an observation was measured and the time it was uploaded. It should also make gaps visible rather than filling them silently with fabricated continuity.
Offline operation introduces another design decision: how much data to buffer and for how long. That depends on the product's latency, privacy, storage, and battery constraints. Not every observation needs to be retained indefinitely, but the policy should be deliberate.
These concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.
Where to start: a practical implementation plan
I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.
- Preserve the evidence. Confirm that raw values, units, source identifiers, measurement timestamps, arrival timestamps, and relevant metadata are captured before transformation.
- Define the temporal contract. Document how observations are aligned, how stale data is handled, and what happens when a required measurement is missing or late.
- Make coordinate assumptions explicit. Identify which calculations depend on phone orientation, how transformations are established, and how uncertainty affects downstream use.
- Introduce a quality contract. Define accept, degrade, and abstain outcomes for one event type. Record reason codes so that quality failures can be distinguished from event-rule failures.
- Validate failure scenarios. Test delayed, missing, duplicated, out-of-order, and contradictory observations. Test phone rotations and changes in sensor availability, not only normal journeys.
- Instrument the pipeline. Track timestamp skew, data freshness, sampling gaps, quality outcomes, event revisions, and end-to-end latency.
- Expand incrementally. Once the chosen event has a defensible processing path, apply the same architectural contracts to other event types, adapting the quality requirements to each use case.
The goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.
What this architecture does not solve
A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.
It cannot recover missing evidence
The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.
It does not replace algorithm validation
The six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.
Quality thresholds are not universal
Freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.
Operational trade-offs remain
Background execution restrictions, battery consumption, connectivity, device diversity, and privacy influence what can be collected and processed. Teams must balance these constraints with evidence requirements and processing latency. They must also define how uncertain outcomes and abstentions are communicated and when additional data or manual review is appropriate.
Ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.
Conclusion: reliability belongs to the pipeline
Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.
The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.
The phantom braking scenario shows why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.
The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

articles.title: Q&A: Mark Darrah on what BioWare’s closure means for the Canadian game industry
articles.text:
Last month, storied Edmonton-based game developer BioWare announced it was being shuttered by parent company Electronic Arts (EA). The closure has left a hole in Alberta’s gaming industry and sparked backlash from fans of the studio’s iconic games. Hundreds of thousands have signed petitions like #SaveMassEffect, while others have advocated for the studio’s sale rather than closure.
Mark Darrah helped build a lot of that fanbase. The former BioWare developer and current video game consultant and YouTuber left the company in 2021 after nearly 25 years of helping produce some of the firm’s biggest titles. In the wake of his former alma mater’s demise, BetaKit caught up with Darrah to talk about why the studio was shut down, his thoughts on EA, and why he thinks ballooning budgets for AAA games could lead to the end of many more gaming studios.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
BioWare was an anchor for gaming in Edmonton, Alberta, and Western Canada. Without it, what gaps are left? Does its loss create an opportunity for other studios?
BioWare was this gravitational force that kind of swept off everything else. There wasn’t really anything else. Now, it feels like there is a more vibrant mid-tier community in Edmonton than before. The thing that BioWare provided that’s now gone is a backstop. If I interview and I decide to relocate to Edmonton and things go belly up and the studio loses its funding, then I could go to BioWare. With that gone, if I move to Edmonton, I’m taking a risk because if my job goes away, I have to try to land at one of the other indie studios that are never hiring many people.
So there’s less stability in the game development market here without BioWare?
Yeah, exactly.
You were with BioWare almost from its beginning. Why did you finally step away in 2021?
Some of it was that my relationship with EA changed in 2017 and we never really came out the other side of that. So, by late 2020, it was just time to go.
I had been treating [EA] as if it was this caring entity, but, of course, it’s not. It’s a corporation, and it’s behaving like a corporation.
How do you navigate between a game publisher doing what’s in its best interest, and seeing those decisions lead to indirectly sabotaging a studio’s creative process?
The fundamental incompatibility between EA and BioWare was that on pretty much all of its projects BioWare grew its way to success. In the early days, when we were struggling to make Baldur’s Gate, we hired 40 more people. After we were acquired by EA, we weren’t allowed to hire people anymore. So what do we do? Well, Dragon Age and Mass Effect need more people to ship. We’ll just eat all the other things we’ve been doing. They’re all gone. After a point, we’ve kind of eaten all the fat off of our studio, and so now, even though our processes still kind of demand this little surge at the end, we weren’t allowed to do it anymore. 
I don’t blame EA for that. That’s just EA; that’s just how they are. Ultimately, that friction was building up in BioWare’s machinery; the studio probably should have been 100 more people than it was, or it should have dropped an entire franchise line, but it did neither, and so that friction was building up until it ultimately kind of resulted in the machinery not really operating properly anymore. 
You mean just focusing on a single game exclusively? What might that have looked like?
When you look at a studio like Maxis, which is also a studio with a culture very different to EA’s, what they did was they effectively became one project, and so the envelope is very much sized to that one project. I wouldn’t have wanted BioWare to do this, but I believe that if it had, it would have slotted into the culture of EA better.
Since the closure, there have been some grassroots efforts to save some of BioWare’s intellectual property. The #SaveMassEffect campaign has hundreds of thousands of signatures. Do you think realistically that EA would ever be open to selling that IP?
If EA was still fully independent, I would say no. A lot of EA’s culture is built around avoiding blame. You can’t think of EA as a single entity, you have to remember it’s built out of a lot of people. What they’re trying to do isn’t make the most money for EA: they’re not trying to make the best decision, they’re not trying to make the best art, they’re trying to avoid someone yelling at them.
If you think about the scenario of taking that IP and selling it for, let’s say, $10 million. EA gets $10 million. Everyone’s happy, right? The thing that the person making that decision is worried about is, if they sell Dragon Age for $10 million, and then the people who buy it make a game that wins Game of the Year, well then someone comes and yells at them, and is like, “why couldn’t we do that?”
EA has been bought out by a Saudi investment company, and EA now has $20 billion USD of debt from that leveraged deal. They’ve got about a billion dollars in profit in a given year. So now the calculus is maybe changed.
In Canada, we’ve seen many recent layoffs and other game studio closures, most notably at Ubisoft. What does the end of BioWare signal about the state of the video-game industry right now?
The fidelity of games has gone up and up, especially in AAA games. You can see the peak of that in Grand Theft Auto VI. Its budget is probably north of a billion dollars. Nobody else can spend that. What I think is starting to happen is you’re starting to see that traditional AAA games are almost moving up into AAAA. The rest of us are going to go the other way, and our budgets have to come down. What we are starting to see signs of is separation. The games right where BioWare sat are starting to go away. The high-budget, but lower-tier AAA games may disappear. Those studios are going to have to drive their budgets down.
I do think that there is a path forward, but I think a bunch of AAA studios are going to essentially not make the cut. They will not be able to pivot. They won’t be able to either become Skyrim or Grand Theft Auto, or figure out how to make their games for less money. There will be a hole, and AA studios will move into that hole.
What impact do you think those higher costs have on the Canadian market?
The problem in Canada is that it’s harder to get $75 million than in San Francisco or New York. If this is what’s happening, if we’re going to turn over the entire industry, then we’re going to lose a bunch of studios, and new studios will rise into the hole in places where they can get funding. That likely leads to studios from the edges of the tree falling away, and more studios rising closer to the trunk. 
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtsey Mark Darrah on YouTube.

articles.title: Confira o Olhar Digital News na íntegra (27/11/2026)
articles.text:
Veja os destaques do Olhar Digital News desta sexta-feira (27/11).
Hackers invadem sistema da Força Aérea dos EUA
Hackers invadiram a Cloud One, principal plataforma de computação em nuvem da Força Aérea dos Estados Unidos, provocando interrupções no sistema. O ataque, confirmado nesta sexta-feira (27), pode comprometer dados sensíveis relacionados a operações militares, pessoal e logística.
Black Friday deve movimentar R$ 11,5 bilhões no Brasil
A Black Friday de 2026 deve movimentar R$ 11,5 bilhões no varejo brasileiro, segundo estimativa é da Confederação Nacional do Comércio de Bens, Serviços e Turismo. Isso representa um crescimento de 1,8% nas vendas em relação ao ano passado, já descontada a inflação. Esse avanço, no entanto, deve ser menor que o registrado em 2025.
OpenAI contra-ataca e acusa Apple de roubar segredos comerciais
A OpenAI abriu uma nova frente na disputa judicial com a Apple. Nesta sexta-feira (27), a empresa responsável pelo ChatGPT apresentou uma ação contra a fabricante do iPhone, acusando a rival de roubar segredos comerciais e dificultar seu acesso a fornecedores de hardware.
NASA quer que robôs façam a manutenção de data centers no espaço
Um estudo da NASA defende que a manutenção de data centers espaciais dependerá principalmente de robôs, e não de equipes de astronautas. A pesquisa aponta que chips utilizados em sistemas de IA ficam obsoletos em três a cinco anos. Isso significa que os computadores instalados no espaço precisarão ser substituídos com frequência, mesmo que o restante do satélite continue funcionando.
Alessandro Di Lorenzo é editor do Olhar Digital e formado em jornalismo pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).

articles.title: Volvo workers are teaching humanoid robots to do their jobs
articles.text:
In a nutshell: More humanoid robots are making their way into automakers' factories. The latest to join the trend is Volvo, which is training humanoid robots at its manufacturing plant in Ghent, Belgium. As is always the case when machines enter the workplace, Volvo claims the idea is for the robots to take on some of the more repetitive and physically demanding jobs, but there's always the specter of replacement in instances like these.
Ghent is the first Volvo plant to try the AEON humanoids, built by Swedish technology group Hexagon. Volvo employees show the robots how to place components precisely into two fixtures, and the machines learn by copying them. Once they can do that reliably, the team will teach them to handle several parts, move around the production area, and work with the plant's automated equipment.
AEON stands about 5 feet 5 inches tall, weighs 132 pounds, and can carry 22 pounds. One decidedly unhuman feature is the set of wheels that can propel it across the factory floor at just over 5 mph. The appeal for Volvo is that AEON can move between workstations designed for people, something a robotic arm bolted to the floor would struggle to do, obviously.
More robots are due in Ghent for a larger pilot in the first half of 2027. Volvo wants them working on the production line by the middle of the year, though it hasn't said how many will join the workforce or what that might mean for the people currently doing those jobs.
In October, Volvo announced plans to cut 2,500 jobs worldwide, including 2,000 in Sweden. The company hasn't linked those cuts to the robot program, but Ghent workers were already waiting to hear what the cost-cutting drive would mean for their plant.
Hyundai's workers have been vocal on the subject of robot replacements. The automaker plans to put Boston Dynamics' Atlas to work at its Georgia factory in 2028, the same year it wants the capacity to build 30,000 robots annually. Hyundai has even floated the idea of selling robots through its dealerships and offering financing to buyers.
Back in January, Hyundai's South Korean union warned of a "huge employment shock" and insisted management would need its agreement before a single robot could be deployed at its worksites. In Ghent, meanwhile, workers are teaching the machines how to do the very jobs they could one day lose to them.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
  November 14, 2026
- Source:
  University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
  Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: CRTC says Bell, Rogers, Telus violated junk fee rules
articles.text:
Amidst the chaos of Black Friday deals, the CRTC published decisions related to carriers’ junk fees and 60-day phone locking schemes.
“Following a public proceeding, the CRTC determined that some providers were in violation of the Telecommunications Act. As a result, it is requiring them to stop charging certain fees by the end of this year. These include fees for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan,” the commission explained in a release on Friday.
“The CRTC also determined that a provider violated consumer protection measures by locking cellphones for up to 60 days. The CRTC will consider whether they should face a penalty of up to $10 million.”
While the CRTC didn’t name the carrier in its initial release, a separate document containing the full decision cites Bell as the carrier that didn’t provide unlocked phones.
Junk fees decision
Let’s start with a bit of context. The CRTC banned junk fees (like connection fees) that carriers charge when customers activate a new line back in June. However, the Big Three — Rogers, Bell, and Telus — moved quickly to introduce new fees they claimed didn’t violate the rules. The CRTC told the carriers to stop and started a review of the new fees, bringing us to today’s decision.
“Based on the record of the proceeding, the Commission finds that the cellphone handling charge from Bell Canada, the cellphone setup charge from Rogers, and the SIM and eSIM provisioning fee from TELUS are prohibited. The Commission also finds that the fees charged by Rogers and TELUS to replace broken or lost SIM cards are not prohibited, nor are the shipping fees charged by Rogers,” the commission said in its decision.
The CRTC specifically called out Bell and Rogers for their respective device handling and setup fees, and Telus for charging SIM and eSIM provisioning fees to new customers. However, the commission also acknowledges that Rogers’ hardware shipping fee, as well as SIM replacement fees, aren’t prohibited under the junk fee rules.
Further, the CRTC directed the Big Three to stop charging the prohibited fees by no later than Dec. 27, 2026. However, that deadline leaves me wondering what will happen for customers who have already had to pay the fees — such as, for example, people shopping Black Friday deals today or Boxing Day deals next month.
Elsewhere in the decision, the CRTC said that it won’t charge administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) at this time, but said it would “continue to actively monitor fees and is ready to take further enforcement action against [providers] that charge prohibited fees.”
Phone locking
The phone locking saga has been going on for some time, dating back years. It largely centres on Bell, though Telus got involved in recent months.
The CRTC banned the practice of locking phones to a network back in 2017, making it much easier (and cheaper!) for Canadians to change wireless providers. However, carriers have criticized the move, in particular claiming it has enabled more theft and fraud.
In April 2025, Bell started locking devices for up to 60 days after activation. The CRTC ordered Bell to stop the practice, but Bell continued. Then, in July 2026, Telus asked the CRTC to pause and permanently change the phone locking rules, claiming that Bell’s 60-day phone lock made its own devices more appealing targets for theft and fraud.
The CRTC issued two decisions related to phone locking. The first was for Bell, in which the commission found “that Bell Canada failed to comply with the Wireless Code” by locking devices for 60 days and is considering fining the carrier.
“The Commission is of the preliminary view that the imposition of an administrative monetary penalty (AMP) of up to $10 million may be appropriate.”
The CRTC has asked for comments on the matter, with a deadline of Jan. 15, 2027. Moreover, Bell can respond by Jan. 22, 2027.
The second decision was directed to Telus over the carrier’s request for a pause on the phone locking rules and ultimately authorization from the CRTC to lock phones for 60 days following activation.
In short, the CRTC denied Telus’ request, noting that it already granted carriers the ability to lock phones for two business days. Further, the commission said that discussions on a permanent change to phone locking rules should take place as part of its ongoing review of the consumer protection codes.
Notably, as part of that review, several carriers have already asked the CRTC to change consumer protections, including the phone locking rules. Other consumer protections carriers sought to have removed include clawbacks for sign-up benefits, roaming caps, and extended financing offers.
