articles.title: The Best Gaming Monitors: Late 2026 Update
articles.text:
Choosing the best gaming monitor has become considerably more interesting in 2026. OLED prices have continued to fall, newer generations of WOLED and QD-OLED panels have brought meaningful improvements to image quality, and there are some genuinely exciting new display formats at the high end. Even budget LCDs are offering a level of performance and features that would have been difficult to find at these prices a couple of years ago, and that's the way it should be.
For our latest gaming monitor buying guide, we've refreshed our recommendations across 8 categories, from flagship 5K2K ultrawides and premium 4K OLEDs to affordable 1440p displays, mini-LED LCDs, and ultra-high-refresh-rate monitors for competitive gaming. We're also introducing a new category for high-resolution monitors that are particularly well suited to a combination of gaming and productivity.
As always, our recommendations are based on extensive hands-on testing, rather than simply comparing spec sheets. Nearly every monitor featured here has been thoroughly reviewed either on TechSpot or over at Monitors Unboxed, with a few recommendations based on closely related models and familiar panel technology. Our dedicated reviews and more specialized buying guides provide a deeper look at the performance of each display.
Whether you're spending $150 or more than $1,000, there are some excellent options available right now. Here's what we'd buy.
The Ultimate Gaming Monitor
Dell Alienware AW3926QW
For the past few updates, we've recommended that flagship monitor buyers purchase a nice, high-end 32-inch 4K OLED. Those are still great products, but a new category in 2026 has taken over this position at the top of the market. In our opinion, the best gaming monitor format right now is the 39-inch 5K2K ultrawide. If you're going to spend over $1,000 on a display, this is where we'd be spending that money.
A 39-inch 5K2K display, with a resolution of 5120x2160 and a 21:9 aspect ratio, is a large, immersive format for gaming. It's the same height as a 32-inch 4K 16:9 monitor, but with an additional 20cm of width, enveloping substantially more of your field of view. The latest models released in 2026 include crucial upgrades that mean they no longer lag behind other high-end panel types. They're finally in a position where we can wholeheartedly recommend them.
The best 39-inch 5K2K OLED monitor is the Dell Alienware AW3926QW, which has just hit a new all-time low price of $1,000. Even at its regular $1,100 MSRP, we think this display is a great buy. It uses a Tandem WOLED panel with an RGB Stripe subpixel layout, has a beautiful glossy finish that preserves deep blacks, and performs really well across most areas. It's actually the monitor I personally use for gaming, and I've gone into considerable detail about why I made that decision in a separate feature.
In our opinion, the best gaming monitor format right now is the 39-inch 5K2K ultrawide. If you're going to spend over $1,000 on a display, this is where we'd be spending that money. It's the same height as a 32-inch 4K 16:9 monitor, but with an additional 20cm of width, enveloping substantially more of your field of view.
The 5K2K resolution is a big upgrade over previous ultrawides of this size, as this level of pixel density is necessary to produce a crisp image on such a huge screen. It uses a pleasant 1500R curve, rather than the overly aggressive 800R curvature found on some competing monitors, and the OLED technology is current-generation Tandem WOLED, the latest from LG Display.
It offers great HDR performance, including decent peak brightness, vibrant colors, true zero-level blacks, and amazing contrast. Dell has also done a wonderful job of calibrating the screen, even offering several useful HDR modes.
As with all products, there are some drawbacks, the main one being its 165Hz refresh rate. We'd have loved to see this monitor offer 240Hz, but currently no 5K2K ultrawide does. Still, as this monitor is designed primarily for immersive single-player experiences, 165Hz is sufficient.
Some aspects of performance are less impressive than we'd have liked, such as panel dimming and uniformity, which you can learn more about in our full review. But these drawbacks aren't significant enough to stop us from recommending the AW3926QW, especially considering its outstanding value at the standard $1,100 asking price.
LG 39GX950B
The other main option at this size is the LG 39GX950B, though the panel itself is different, with LG opting for the RGWB subpixel version and a matte screen coating.
The LG model is still a great monitor, but we don't think it performs as well as the Dell overall, and it's more expensive. Unless you specifically want a feature the LG offers, we'd just get the AW3926QW. Make sure to update the firmware if you do end up purchasing one, though, as the latest version includes some crucial fixes.
Best Premium 4K Gaming Monitor
Gigabyte Aorus FO32U24G | Asus ROG XG32UQWMS
If you're after a high-end gaming monitor in the $700 to $900 range, or simply don't want a massive 39-inch ultrawide, this is where we think a 32-inch 4K 240Hz OLED makes sense. These are fantastic displays, offering a large screen size, high resolution and refresh rate, plus all the latest benefits of OLED technology.
There are so many 32-inch 4K OLED panel options right now, including WOLED and QD-OLED variants spanning several generations of each technology. No option is perfect, as both WOLED and QD-OLED have their strengths and weaknesses, but we think the best option for most people right now is a Tandem WOLED display using the RGWB subpixel layout. This is the very latest generation of the technology, found in displays that have only just hit the market.
No option is perfect, as both WOLED and QD-OLED have their strengths and weaknesses, but we think the best option for most people right now is Tandem WOLED.
This panel offers a combination of strengths that sets it apart from competing QD-OLEDs and other WOLED formats. One major advantage is the screen coating. Tandem WOLED is available with a glossy finish that does a fantastic job of preserving deep blacks across a range of lighting conditions.
Gigabyte Aorus Elite FO32U24G
Another advantage is more consistent HDR brightness across both bright and dark scenes: you won't find panel dimming here. This leads to better-looking HDR without having to constantly fiddle with the settings. You also get dual-mode functionality, offering a 1080p 480Hz configuration that increases motion clarity compared to the standard 4K 240Hz mode, making it suitable for fast-paced competitive gaming.
Aside from these competitive advantages, the WOLED RGWB panel is just fantastic, and the monitors using it are excellent. You get the usual exceptionally fast response times, great color calibration, high HDR brightness, and strong feature sets.
This 2026 panel is used in both the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS and Gigabyte Aorus Elite FO32U24G. We've tested both and found the Gigabyte model to be slightly better, but both monitors are great buys in our opinion. The Asus model has been available for as little as $700 on sale, which is an exceptionally good deal, but even its $900 MSRP is reasonable.
What about QD-OLED alternatives?
You should buy a QD-OLED instead if you don't want to deal with Tandem WOLED's biggest flaw: dark gray banding. Choosing to avoid this issue comes with a trade-off, of course, as QD-OLED has its own set of issues, including raised blacks and HDR panel dimming. But some buyers find the gray banding on WOLEDs extremely annoying, so if you think this will be a deal-breaker for you, just get a QD-OLED. We'd also recommend a QD-OLED if you want higher color brightness and a less reflective screen coating.
The other reason to get a QD-OLED is pricing. The XG32UQWMS is a great buy at $700 and one of the cheapest 32-inch 4K OLEDs on the market at that price. But it's not always available for $700, given its $900 MSRP.
Gigabyte MO32U24
In those situations, QD-OLED can be cheaper, with models like the MSI 321UPX starting at $700 and the Gigabyte MO32U24 offering a newer generation panel at $800. These are worth considering if Tandem WOLED options are too expensive in your region. As they're still 32-inch 4K 240Hz models, they offer the same motion clarity and all the usual benefits of OLED's per-pixel control.
Lastly, it's worth noting that in the first quarter of 2027, Samsung Display will be releasing a new generation of 32-inch 4K panels equipped with a 360Hz refresh rate and upgraded brightness. It could be worth waiting for these new monitors if you're planning on buying something high-end.
We expect pricing to start north of $1,000, so they might not be overly competitive with existing $800 Tandem WOLEDs or QD-OLEDs, but the specifications revealed so far are tantalizing.
Best 1440p OLED Gaming
Gigabyte MO27Q28GR
The best mid-range gaming monitors on the market right now are 1440p OLEDs, and you won't need to break the bank to get one. While we generally consider the mid-range of the monitor market to be around $500, you can now pick up some very good 1440p OLEDs for around $400, occasionally even less if you find a particularly good deal.
As with the 32-inch 4K category, at 1440p you need to choose between a WOLED or QD-OLED panel, and the pros and cons of each type are similar to what we discussed in the previous section. We've covered the differences in detail in a separate feature, but as with 32-inch 4K models, we generally believe that 1440p Tandem WOLED panels are the best overall.
The best mid-range gaming monitors on the market right now are 1440p OLEDs, and you won't need to break the bank to get one.
Our primary recommendation in this category is the Gigabyte MO27Q28GR, a 27-inch 1440p 280Hz WOLED using the latest generation of panel technology. While normally priced around $500, you can grab this display for less than $430 right now. The GR model that we'd recommend to most people uses a fantastic glossy screen coating, but you can save a small amount by going with a matte coating instead, as Gigabyte's MO27Q28G is just $400 right now. The G and GR variants are virtually identical in performance outside of the differences in screen coating.
The MO27Q28GR provides great brightness across SDR and HDR modes, typically offering a brighter experience than competing QD-OLEDs. HDR brightness is also much more consistent between different types of scenes, as there's no QD-OLED-like panel dimming. This means you get a combination of higher peak brightness in favorable conditions, and more impactful, accurate HDR in brighter scenes. It's a significant factor in why we recommend Tandem WOLED and why we prefer its HDR experience.
The Gigabyte models offer a good set of features, including black frame insertion, an anti-flicker mode, USB-C input, and a KVM switch. They also perform well in color accuracy tests and offer excellent motion clarity thanks to their 280Hz refresh rate.
Asus ROG Strix XG27AQWMG
The Asus ROG Strix XG27AQWMG is another option that performs very well, and we've seen it for just $400 when on sale. However, its standard price of $650 is higher than the Gigabyte models. It's not significantly better, so we'd get whichever model is cheaper.
More affordable 1440p QD-OLEDs
Again, 1440p QD-OLEDs are a suitable alternative in this category if you don't like the idea of dark gray banding, want higher color brightness or lower reflectivity, or simply want to save some money. In some regions, the price difference is substantially in favor of QD-OLED, so be sure to check the full range of options available to you.
Dell Alienware AW2725D
We can comfortably recommend the Dell Alienware AW2725D at just $350. This is a 27-inch 1440p 280Hz QD-OLED model that uses the full-brightness panel from Samsung Display.
Usually in this price range we only see the limited-brightness QD-OLED Edge panels, which are a bit of a trap as they only offer 400 nits of HDR brightness instead of 1,000 nits. But at least right now, the AW2725D is $350, which is an absolute steal and an all-time low price.
The AW2725D is one of our favorite models to use the 280Hz panel, and it recently performed well in our budget 1440p QD-OLED roundup. It offers solid calibration, a good refresh rate, strong HDR brightness, and a great design.
Even with the Alienware at just $350, we'd still lean toward Tandem WOLED at $400 to $430, as we think those panels are better overall. But this is an amazing bang-for-your-buck product if you can't quite stretch your budget that far or would be annoyed by dark gray banding.
Gigabyte MO27Q2A
One alternative to the AW2725D that has consistently been available at a great price over the last few months is the Gigabyte MO27Q2A, which uses the same 1440p 280Hz QD-OLED panel. While we haven't tested this specific model, we're familiar with how the panel performs and have been impressed with the quality of Gigabyte's recent displays, so we're comfortable recommending it.
For really budget-conscious shoppers who can't justify spending $350 or $400 on a gaming monitor, this is where the limited-brightness QD-OLED panels make more sense. We'd want a decent discount, though. Right now, with the AW2725D at $350, it's hard to justify saving just $50 to grab a 240Hz model that doesn't properly display HDR content.
The Gigabyte GO27Q24A, for example, is a great choice among displays that use the limited-brightness panel, but at $300 we'd just spend the extra $50 to grab the 280Hz Alienware.
Alienware AW2726DM
The Alienware AW2726DM is approaching the sort of price range where it makes sense to grab a dirt-cheap QD-OLED, as it's currently available at an all-time low of $280. However, these discounts may not last, so as a general rule, we'd want to see at least a 20% price gap between limited-brightness and full-brightness models. You can learn about several other options in our recent budget QD-OLED roundup.
Best 4K Mini-LED Gaming Monitor
MSI 274URDFW E16M | Koorui S2741LM
Something we regularly hear from a subset of our readers is that they want to spend $300 to $500 on a monitor capable of gaming, but for one reason or another don't want to purchase an OLED. And there are several valid reasons for that.
If you do a lot of productivity work on your display, the prospect of OLED burn-in over time is not ideal. You may want a higher resolution than 1440p, but can't justify spending at least $600 on a 27-inch 4K OLED. Or maybe you want to enjoy HDR gaming with a ton of brightness and punch, in which case a mini-LED LCD is a great option.
If you're after a mid-range LCD monitor priced between $300 and $500, we'd generally recommend a 27-inch 4K mini-LED LCD. You can also purchase 1440p displays with refresh rates of 300Hz or higher in this category, but on balance, we think 4K mini-LED makes the most sense, especially if you're looking for a hybrid gaming and productivity display.
MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M
Late last year, we tested several 27-inch 4K mini-LED LCDs in a dedicated roundup and found that all of them were great buys, with a variety of strengths depending on the product in question. It's well worth checking out that roundup for more details, but in short, right now we'd be looking at either the MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M or the Koorui S2741LM, both of which are available for $400. The MSI's regular price is on the higher end, normally around $500, but at $400 it's a much better buy.
Both models use a 27-inch 4K IPS LCD panel with a 160Hz refresh rate and a 1,152-zone mini-LED backlight. With full-array local dimming, these 4K LCDs are genuinely capable of displaying HDR images properly, unlike fake HDR products that lack local dimming and are often labeled with misleading "HDR 400" specifications.
Koorui S2741LM
Having 1,152 backlight zones allows for a substantial increase in contrast over SDR monitors, with deeper blacks and decent control over individual areas of the screen, meaning bright and dark elements can be displayed at the same time. This creates the dazzling, impressive HDR effect that you're paying for. It's not simply a matter of running the screen at a higher brightness level.
Having 1,000+ backlight zones gets you the impressive HDR effect you're paying for. It's not simply a matter of running the screen at a higher brightness level. In the right circumstances, these LCDs can look remarkably similar to an OLED.
Speaking of brightness, these monitors are capable of some very impressive results, especially in brighter scenes. The Koorui achieves over 1,600 nits in real-scene tests. Along with good shadow detail and a fast dimming response, we get solid performance for HDR gaming that takes things to the next level relative to cheaper SDR products. In the right circumstances, these LCDs can look remarkably similar to an OLED.
Motion performance is pretty good across these models. They're typical fast IPS panels, with different levels of optimization depending on the model you get. The 1080p 320Hz dual mode increases motion clarity for multiplayer gaming, making these quite versatile products: HDR gaming in single-player titles, 320Hz gaming in multiplayer titles, and productivity work without the risk of burn-in.
AOC U27G4XM
The AOC U27G4XM is also an option at just $350, though we don't think it's quite as good as the MSI or Koorui models. Whether or not the $50 saving is worth it depends entirely on whether you prioritize value or performance. The AOC model performs well, so we still recommend it, but the others have stronger feature sets.
Best Affordable Gaming Monitors
Gigabyte M27Q2 QD | AOC Q27G40XMN
Good news for anyone shopping for a budget gaming monitor: we recently published a roundup looking at nine different 27-inch 1440p LCDs, all priced below $200. That's by far the best resource for exploring which entry-level option you should buy, and it goes into considerably more detail than we'll cover here. Of the options we've tested, there are two standouts.
The Gigabyte M27Q2 QD, or M27Q2 SA in some regions, is a fantastic $160 gaming monitor offering a 1440p 210Hz IPS LCD panel. It has a wider color gamut than most of its competitors and better response time tuning, including variable overdrive and a single overdrive mode experience. It also has a height-adjustable stand with excellent overall build quality, both USB-C and a KVM switch, which are rare in this price tier, and a good set of gaming features. The only drawback is that color calibration isn't as strong as on the best models.
Other monitors priced around $160 might match the M27Q2 QD in a couple of areas, but not as a complete package. Some might have comparable response time tuning but only offer a fixed-height stand. Others might be better calibrated but have a smaller color gamut and a limited port selection.
It's the balance of performance, a strong feature set, and excellent design that makes the M27Q2 QD our go-to choice.
Best Value HDR option
The other option we highly recommend is the AOC Q27G40XMN. This is the clear winner if you want a display with HDR, and for a lot of gamers it's probably what we'd recommend overall, especially for those who primarily play single-player games. It's one of very few models at $200 that offer true HDR capabilities, thanks to a 1,152-zone backlight and brightness output approaching 1,400 nits.
AOC Q27G40XMN
There are some caveats, though. It has a fixed-height stand, which is disappointing. Response time performance is average at best, although not too bad considering it's a VA LCD panel, and viewing angles are weak relative to the IPS alternatives. But it has an amazing contrast ratio, deep blacks, and real HDR capabilities. It's definitely a product to consider if it's available in your region.
There were other models in our roundup that we found to be reasonable and could be worth considering depending on pricing in your region. These include the LG 27G610A, KTC H27T6, and Asus TUF Gaming VG27AQL5A. Check out the full roundup for more information. However, if these products are the same price or more expensive than the Gigabyte M27Q2 QD, just get the Gigabyte. It's the better monitor.
Best for Competitive Gaming
G-Sync Pulsar | MSI MAG 272QP X50
A lot of the monitors in this buying guide so far have been all-rounder picks, suitable for many use cases, or even leaning toward single-player gaming. But if you primarily play competitive multiplayer games and want to prioritize motion clarity, input latency, and speed, we have a different set of recommendations catering specifically to those characteristics.
There are essentially two ways you can go here. A G-Sync Pulsar monitor is a great choice if you want the absolute best motion clarity. The other main choice is an ultra-high-refresh-rate OLED monitor, which might be the best option if you want speed while retaining the image quality and HDR benefits of an OLED display.
G-Sync Pulsar
G-Sync Pulsar is revolutionary because it allows you to use backlight strobing and variable refresh simultaneously. If you're not familiar with backlight strobing, it's a technology that pulses the backlight on and off between refresh cycles, instead of holding the image on screen for the full cycle. This impulse-based approach significantly reduces persistence blur. When your eyes track objects across the screen, the impulse essentially performs some visual trickery, allowing your brain to perceive the object with greater clarity.
G-Sync Pulsar is flawless in how it handles variable refresh, giving you the full benefit of strobing across its supported variable refresh rate range. You no longer have to run games at a specific fixed refresh rate and disable crucial features to get the best motion clarity.
This has big benefits in games where motion clarity is important, like fast-paced shooters, racing games, and anything that requires tracking enemies, objects, or even text in motion.
In our testing earlier this year, we found that 1440p 360Hz G-Sync Pulsar displays look clearer than OLEDs at high refresh rates, and much clearer at moderate to lower refresh rates.
This makes Pulsar the clearer technology in a wide range of situations, whether you're playing lightweight games that run at really high frame rates or typically play at, say, 120 fps. And Pulsar just works in all these situations. You enable it and away you go, with no need for further configuration.
As for specific monitors, there are four G-Sync Pulsar options on the market: the Asus ROG Strix Pulsar XG27AQNGV, MSI MPG 272QRF X36, AOC Agon Pro AG276QSG2, and Acer Predator XB273U F5. We're still working on full reviews of the Asus and MSI models, but all four use the same panel and offer the same G-Sync Pulsar functionality. The Asus and MSI models seem very solid based on what we've seen so far, and both have been available for less than $400, which is a fantastic price given that they debuted above $600 earlier this year.
Ultra-high-refresh-rate OLEDs
An alternative to G-Sync Pulsar is a high-refresh-rate OLED. This will be a better option if you'd prefer the superior image quality of an OLED panel versus an IPS LCD, want proper HDR functionality, or don't have an Nvidia GeForce GPU, as that's required for Pulsar.
If you're sensitive to the flicker of backlight strobing, you may also find OLED more comfortable to view, although OLED still exhibits a slight, rapid flicker during normal operation that causes eye strain for a tiny percentage of people.
Asus ROG Swift PG27AQWP-W
The best high-refresh-rate OLED is the Asus ROG Swift PG27AQWP-W, which uses a 27-inch 1440p 540Hz Tandem WOLED panel. This is a very similar display to the 280Hz Tandem WOLEDs we discussed in an earlier section, except with the refresh rate increased to 540Hz. It also offers a 720p 720Hz dual mode, which you might find useful in some situations, though I generally found the resolution to be too low.
While 540Hz Tandem WOLED is the best option in this category, the Asus model is extremely expensive at over $1,000. For most people, we think opting for a 500Hz QD-OLED makes a lot more sense, as they're priced closer to $500 to $600 these days.
MSI MAG 272QP X50
We'd be looking at the MSI MAG 272QP X50, and you can learn more about the available options in several of our other features, including our 500Hz monitor roundup and our dedicated 1440p and OLED buying guides.
High-refresh-rate 1080p OLEDs have also come onto the market over the last month or so, targeting hardcore competitive gamers who love the 24.5-inch display format. They're worth exploring as well, and we'll be reviewing them shortly.
Best Ultrawides: 34" and Larger
Dell Alienware AW3426DW | Alienware AW3926QW
The best ultrawide category is fairly straightforward. The ultimate choice is the Dell Alienware AW3926QW, which we already covered in the best flagship monitor section. If you're after a 39-inch ultrawide panel, that's the one to get.
But there are several other excellent options if you want a different panel size. In the 34-inch category, the best monitors right now use the latest 3440x1440 QD-OLED panel, released this year with an RGB Stripe subpixel layout and improvements to brightness and screen coating. This panel is primarily available in two versions, one with a 280Hz refresh rate and one with a 360Hz refresh rate. Our testing has shown these panels to be identical in performance outside of the refresh rate.
Naturally, the 360Hz version is better because of its higher refresh rate, making it the best overall option on the market at this size in terms of performance. But there's usually a decent price difference between the 360Hz and 280Hz models, which makes the 280Hz versions better value and ultimately the better buy in most situations.
MSI MPG 341CQR X36
For example, the MSI MPG 341CQR X36 is a great 360Hz variant that costs $900 these days. If you really want the highest refresh rate, it's the option we'd get. It's even been on sale for as little as $800, but is currently out of stock at that price. The 280Hz variants, which aren't that much slower, are available for just $650, though. The Dell Alienware AW3426DW is a monitor we've tested that offers excellent performance and recently dropped to an all-time low of $650, so that's the model we'd be looking at.
The MSI 341CQP X28 and Asus XG34WCDMS are also products to look out for. With the 280Hz models, you could potentially save over 25% by shaving a bit off the refresh rate for what is otherwise the same QD-OLED panel experience.
Going even bigger: 45-inch ultrawides
If you're interested in a larger ultrawide, our recommendation here is unchanged: the best 45-inch OLED ultrawide is still the LG 45GX950A. It has a massive 45-inch 5120x2160 WOLED panel running at 165Hz, providing an incredible level of immersion. We're not as fond of this monitor as we are of the 39-inch alternatives, as it's using slightly older panel technology and a more aggressive 800R curve.
LG 45GX950A
But it's still a decent display for those building simulator rigs or other setups that require a huge monitor.
Best 5K and 6K Monitors for Gaming and Productivity
LG 27GM950B | Samsung Odyssey G80HS
Our final category is a new addition to this buying guide: high-resolution monitors. By that we mean resolutions higher than 4K, which these days has become a fairly standard option in the premium segment.
You might be wondering why someone would even want a higher-than-4K monitor for gaming, but the primary reason actually has little to do with gaming. Higher resolutions like 5K and 6K offer greater pixel densities and more screen real estate, which is even better for productivity work. Once you get above 200 PPI on a desktop monitor, the image is remarkably crisp, with exceptionally sharp text.
High-DPI displays don't normally provide significant benefits specifically for gaming, but the latest high-resolution monitors have a few tricks up their sleeves that make them great choices as dual-use displays.
LG 27GM950B
For a start, new products released in 2026 finally offer decent refresh rates at their native resolutions. The Samsung Odyssey G80HS and LG 27GM950B are native 6K 165Hz and 5K 165Hz displays, respectively. These are refresh rates that are actually suitable for gaming and offer huge improvements in smoothness for productivity work.
Once you've upgraded from a 60Hz display to a 165Hz display, you'll never want to go back to 60Hz again, regardless of what you're doing.
Once you've upgraded from a 60Hz display to a 165Hz display, you'll never want to go back to 60Hz again, regardless of what you're doing. Most gamers probably won't want to deal with the performance costs of gaming at 5K or 6K, even if the refresh rate is 165Hz. It's a great experience in lightweight games where you can enjoy the exceptionally high resolution, but most AAA titles are difficult to run at these resolutions, especially 6K.
Samsung Odyssey G80HS
However, both models offer a 330Hz dual mode that runs at a lower resolution, purpose-built for gaming. On the 27GM950B it's 1440p 330Hz, and on the G80HS it's 3K 330Hz. Both 1440p and 3K are great resolutions for gaming and are significantly less demanding on GPU hardware. This is where these monitors become great choices for a mixture of productivity and gaming.
You can use the 5K or 6K modes in desktop applications, benefiting from the exceptionally high resolution and screen real estate, then switch to the 1440p or 3K modes for higher-performance gaming without sacrificing too much image clarity. It all works surprisingly well and finally brings high-DPI panels into the modern era of gaming monitors.
The LG 27GM950B is the 5K 165Hz option we've tested. It uses a 27-inch IPS LCD panel and has a mini-LED backlight with 2,304 zones, so it offers proper HDR functionality. It's a great option, but when we reviewed it, we found the $1,200 MSRP to be a bit high, considering some 4K OLEDs are half the price. These days, though, it's available for $800, which is much more reasonable if the combination of a 5K panel and mini-LED backlight sounds appealing.
Samsung Odyssey G80HS
The Samsung Odyssey G80HS is a 6K 165Hz model using a 32-inch IPS LCD panel. It has a similar pixel density to the 5K model, but at a larger screen size. Unfortunately, Samsung's design does not include a mini-LED backlight, which is a bit of a letdown considering the high price, but it's essentially the only 6K panel suitable for gaming right now. As with the LG, we thought its MSRP of $1,600 was far too high, but these days it will set you back just $1,100, putting it in a much better position.
We don't expect either of these monitors to be at the top of most people's lists when shopping for a gaming display. But for those who want the exceptional text clarity of a high-DPI productivity monitor without giving up the speed and responsiveness of a modern gaming display, it's great to finally see these sorts of options debut in 2026.

articles.title: Meet the teen founders turning wealth mogging into a fast-growing startup
articles.text:
LarpGPT came to co-founder and CEO Feiyang Luo earlier this year in a dream. The 19-year-old entrepreneur bought the domain when he woke up.
At first, LarpGPT was just a name—specifically, an amalgamation of LARP, an acronym for live-action role-playing that in some circles has come to mean pretending to be wealthy online, and GPT, a popular family of AI models OpenAI developed for generating text and images.
Luo was attracted to the notion of merging AI with the world of “internet money,” which he said consists of young people who are trying to make money online by doing things like dropshipping, investing in cryptocurrency, and building software, and who often like to aura farm by flaunting their wealth publicly.
“I think the greatest deficit to an ambitious person is being around unambitious people.”
Anthony Li, LarpGPT
The day Luo purchased LarpGPT.com, his 17-year-old friend Anthony Li (LarpGPT’s co-founder and CMO) supplied the initial business idea: an AI-powered image generator that would allow users to envision themselves next to expensive cars, jewellery, and other luxury goods. The pair launched this tool in March and began generating revenue through subscriptions.
Since then, Toronto-based LarpGPT has evolved into a free, head-to-head game that they rolled out this June where young internet hustlers and other players from around the globe “flex” on each other by showing off what they already own. Users battle to present more valuable possessions than their opponent based on specific prompts—say, who has the taller stack of luxury watches on their wrist—and LarpGPT leverages AI to appraise the items shown and determine a winner.
Its premise has quickly taken off. LarpGPT has amassed more than one million users, who are now competing in about 200,000 of these battles daily, and has grown to 10 employees.
From high school debate to flexing online
Gen Z and Gen Alpha are the world’s first internet-native generations. Their members also think a lot differently about money. Amid rising inflation and housing costs, a precarious job market, and unprecedented digital connectivity and exposure to social media, many have turned to the internet to make money outside of traditional work, achieve financial independence, and secure social validation; some have even gone broke in the process.
Luo and Li have been playing around with tech and hustling online for years. Luo is a former SoundCloud rapper who connected with Li, a champion debater, in high school debate club. Li was coding his own sports-betting algorithm, and had built a web scraper capable of pulling odds.
Last year, while finishing Grade 12, Luo claimed he repurposed that scraper to help successfully defend his realtor mother, Yan, against a Real Estate Council of Ontario ethics claim, leveraging the tech to predict arguments and outcomes based on past precedents and build a case around them.
Luo and Li initially teamed up to repurpose old books and build a network to distribute them to prisons across Ontario, securing support from the University of Waterloo for the project and ultimately providing reading material to more than 1,000 inmates. Luo went on to study philosophy at the University of Waterloo before dropping out to pursue LarpGPT with Li, who likewise abandoned high school to focus fully on the startup.
Early results indicate their bet is on a path to paying off. The startup recently secured $1 million USD ($1.4 million CAD) in pre-seed financing from the University of Waterloo’s Velocity incubator, and Silicon Valley’s Afore Capital and Parable VC, among others, to help sustain its rapid growth and support its plan to build LarpGPT into what its founders described as “LinkedIn for internet money.”
LarpGPT’s pre-seed financing, which was raised via simple agreements for future equity (SAFEs) at a $15-million USD ($21.6-million CAD) valuation cap, closed a month ago and marks the startup’s first external financing to date.
Connecting “young hustlers”
In a joint interview with BetaKit, Luo and Li said they hope to cultivate and inspire a community of like-minded “young hustlers” through LarpGPT.
“I think the greatest deficit to an ambitious person is being around unambitious people,” Li said. “When we put these ambitious people together, they really blossom.”
LarpGPT has some pretty grand ambitions. “In the next five years, there’s going to be an entire generation that was inspired and raised on LARP battles [who] look back [on] themselves and say, ‘Wow, I used to see these Lamborghinis on LARP battles; now I have them in person. LARP battles made me a better person and a better hustler.’ That’s the vision,” Li said.
While it’s a grand plan, the pair is also not taking themselves or the games they enable too seriously. Like much of what happens on the internet now, “At the end of the day, it’s all for fun,” Li said. “It’s all for jokes.”
While LarpGPT’s image generator is still available, its game has rapidly become its main attraction. Initial battles and rematches each last 30 seconds, and LarpGPT lets players stay in touch with their competitors outside of matches through its chat and connections features—a key draw for many users.
“In the next five years, there’s going to be an entire generation that was inspired and raised on LARP battles… That’s the vision.”
Anthony Li,
LarpGPT
LarpGPT claims its users range from billionaires to people living in huts with an internet connection. Luo and Li believe every player has something of value to provide, and view the chance to connect folks from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds as a net positive—even if it’s through an arguably silly mechanism. They claimed one user from Kenya earned enough money from streaming his battles and jobs he obtained via viewers to attend university. Luo and Li did not share how LarpGPT itself plans to make money from its game at this time.
While they strive to limit toxicity on LarpGPT, Luo and Li also appreciate that the platform may not be for everyone. If you’re discouraged rather than motivated after playing LarpGPT, you may fall into this boat, Li said. “It’s just what you make of it,” he added.
Establishing your sense of self-worth by comparing yourself to other people online can be harmful to mental health, especially for younger people, and this is part of why Canada is proposing a youth social media ban. When asked how LarpGPT is considering its potential impact in this context, Luo noted that young people “are more capable of learning than at any other time in their lives.”
“I’d say that neuroplasticity, paired with connecting with and absorbing knowledge from others in the internet money space, is a superpower,” Luo said. “Either they wait to see that reality in adulthood, once their youthful drive has been shattered, or we accelerate the spirit of youth and show them that owning a supercar is certainly possible.”
Feature image courtesy LarpGPT.

articles.title: Só na Black Friday: iPhone Air despenca 53% no Mercado Livre
articles.text:
Só na Black Friday: iPhone Air despenca 53% no Mercado Livre
iPhone Air tem A19 Pro e RAM de 12 GB na ficha técnica, que o posicionam em um lugar vantajoso contra o iPhone 17, que é seu concorrente de preço
O iPhone Air (256 GB) está disponível por R$ 5.129 no Pix com o cupom DESCONTABF300 no Mercado Livre. O ultrafino da Apple está com 53% de desconto frente ao preço oficial de R$ 10.999, e agora sai por um valor bem mais realista para a ficha técnica. Hoje, seu concorrente mais próximo em oferta é o iPhone 17.
Comparando os dois modelos, o iPhone Air sai na frente em desempenho, graças ao chip A19 Pro e à RAM de 12 GB. Porém, o celular da Apple em promoção tem menos câmeras (apesar de todas de 48 MP) e bateria inferior. Vale conferir as diferenças entre os produtos abaixo pra ver o que mais vale a pena no seu caso,
O menor preço que já encontramos para o iPhone Air 256 GB foi R$ 5.039, na Black Friday de 2026 (Mercado Livre). Fora de datas promocionais, esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos.
Trazendo o Apple Intelligence, o iPhone Air usa o chipset Apple A19 Pro combinado com 12 GB de RAM, configuração superior comparada ao chip A19 padrão e 8 GB de RAM do iPhone 17. Os 256 GB de armazenamento interno podem exigir o uso do iCloud para ter mais espaço para mídias, aplicativos e outros aplicativos.
A uma tela Super Retina XDR OLED de 6,5 polegadas com o design Dynamic Island e proteção Ceramic Shield também ligeiramente maior que é do iPhone 17 (6,3”). O painel atua com taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho máximo de 3.000 nits, além de usar os recursos ProMotion e HDR para reproduzir imagens detalhadas.
O celular traz uma câmera traseira com um único sensor de 48 MP, mas pronto para registrar fotos com Estabilização Óptica de Imagem (OIS) e filmar vídeo em 4K. Já a câmera frontal de 18 MP fica responsável por selfies detalhadas com o Modo Retrato e vídeo em 4K.
O smartphone mais fino da Apple tem apenas 5,64 mm de espessura, estrutura reforçada em titânio e acabamento traseiro em vidro com Ceramic Shield. O certificado IP68 de resistência à poeira e à água protege o aparelho de mergulhos de até 6 metros em água doce por 30 minutos.
O tamanho compacto reflete na bateria de 3.149 mAh com autonomia para até 27 horas de reprodução de vídeo, três horas a menos de tempo de uso comparado ao iPhone 17. No entanto, o carregamento rápido de 20 W vai de 0 a 50% em apenas 30 minutos na tomada.
O iPhone Air (R$ 5.129 no Pix com o cupom DESCONTABF300) vem de fábrica com o iOS 26 e receberá ao menos 5 grandes atualizações do sistema operacional. Ademais, o dispositivo tem conexões 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, Ultra Wideband (UWB), NFC.
A Black Friday acontece nesta sexta-feira, 27 de novembro, mas as promoções e cupons de descontos estão sendo liberados desde o começo da semana. Então, siga o Achados do TB no WhatsApp ou no Telegram para não perder nenhuma oferta de celulares, TVs, notebooks e outros eletrônicos.

articles.title: YouTube sur Android Auto : cette nouveauté vidéo va tout changer en voiture
articles.text:
Regarder YouTube au volant va être possible avant l'heure. Enfin, à condition que la voiture soit à l'arrêt, naturellement.
Morphe est un outil open source qui modifie des applications Android pour y ajouter des fonctions ou en retirer la publicité (YouTube, YouTube Music et d'autres services de streaming), est disponible en version 2.4.0. Cette mise à jour concerne les versions modifiées de Reddit, de YouTube et de YouTube Music. La principale nouveauté ici, c'est la lecture de vidéos YouTube sur Android Auto.
YouTube dans le lanceur d'Android Auto
D'après les notes de version, un nouveau correctif permet à une version de YouTube modifié par Morphe d'être reconnue comme une « application vidéo pour véhicule à l'arrêt ». L'application apparaît alors dans le tiroir d'applications d'Android Auto, et il est possible de regarder des vidéos, tant que la voiture ne roule pas. La fonction est pour l'instant proposée en accès anticipé. Elle est aussi compatible avec DriveDeck.
Justement, Google travaille de son côté sur une fonctionnalité comparable pour les smartphones sous Android 17 ou version ultérieure. Cette mise à jour, officielle cette fois-ci, est attendue d'ici la fin de l'année.
Aujourd'hui, sur Android Auto, les utilisateurs peuvent seulement écouter le son des vidéos YouTube, et l'application doit être pilotée depuis le téléphone qui est, on le rappelle, interdit au volant et désormais passible de retrait de permis.
D'autres correctifs concernent l'affichage. L'un détecte quand YouTube est affiché sur l'écran du véhicule et adapte la disposition aux écrans horizontaux. Un autre masque la barre de navigation pour mieux exploiter l'espace disponible. Morphe permet également à des alternatives à Android Auto, comme DriveDeck, Gearslip, AARE et Flywheel, de parcourir la bibliothèque de YouTube Music.
Un mode Ghost et d'autres changements
La mise à jour apporte aussi des modifications qui ne sont pas liées à Android Auto. Le changement majeur est un mode Ghost, comparable à la navigation privée. Les vidéos regardées n'apparaissent pas dans l'historique et n'influencent ainsi pas les recommandations. Il peut être activé pour toute une session, ou pour une seule vidéo via le bouton à trois points, sans déconnexion du compte.
Côté YouTube Music, les paroles peuvent maintenant s'afficher en plein écran, avec la prise en charge de polices personnalisées. Il est également possible de désactiver les gestes qui font changer de morceau en glissant le doigt sur la pochette. Un bouton de diffusion direct vers Sonos a enfin été ajouté. Il permet d'envoyer le son vers des enceintes UPnP de Sonos ou d'autres marques, à condition qu'elles soient connectées au même réseau Wi-Fi.
Source : Android Authority

articles.title: Série noire aux États-Unis : des pirates se sont infiltrés dans Cloud One, la plateforme cloud géante de l’US Air Force
articles.text:
L’intrusion dans le cloud de l’armée de l’air américaine a été repérée il y a environ un mois, au cours de travaux de mise à niveau du système, selon deux des sources de Reuters.
D’après une dépêche du 27 novembre de l’agence de presse Reuters, qui s’appuie sur cinq sources anonymes, des pirates ont réussi à pénétrer Cloud One, la plateforme cloud phare de l’US Air Force.
Lancée en 2017 avec Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle et Alphabet, elle fait tourner des dizaines d’applications, de la paie à la logistique, mais aussi des outils sensibles comme celui qui rassemble les données radar de défense aérienne de toute l’Amérique du Nord.
Les pirates ont atteint le cœur de la plateforme
Interrogée par Reuters, l’Air Force a seulement répondu qu’elle ne commentait pas « la posture de sécurité, les vulnérabilités ou l’état opérationnel » de ses réseaux. Les détails recueillis par l’agence de presse restent maigres. On ne sait ni qui sont les pirates, ni jusqu’où ils sont allés, ni si des données ont été volées.
D’après une des sources de Reuters, les attaquants ont exploité une vulnérabilité logicielle pour atteindre le « control plane », la couche d’administration du cloud, qu’elle compare à une télécommande universelle. Un tel accès permettrait en théorie de consulter l’état opérationnel des avions militaires ou de suivre les mouvements de pièces détachées, sans que l’on sache si les pirates l’ont fait.
Signe de la gravité de l’incident, le Cyber Command, le commandement militaire américain chargé du cyberespace, a été appelé pour évaluer les dégâts. La découverte de l’intrusion a aussi entraîné la suspension de la migration des applications administratives vers Cloud One et le blocage des mises à jour de celles qui y tournaient déjà.
Les agences fédérales américaines enchaînent les piratages
Il s’agit d’une attaque de plus contre l’État fédéral en l’espace d’une semaine. Le 24 novembre, le New York Times révélait la compromission d’un système OSINT de la CIA, qui aurait aussi touché le Bureau du directeur du renseignement national (ODNI) et la National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. Le FinCEN, la cellule de renseignement financier du Trésor, enquête de son côté sur un accès non autorisé, tandis que le NCIC, le fichier criminel national géré par le FBI et partagé par les polices locales, des États et fédérales, aurait lui aussi été piraté, selon des informations de CNN relayées par BleepingComputer.

articles.title: Black Friday: Diese Apple-, Samsung- und Fritz-Deals lohnen sich
articles.text:
Black Friday: Alle guten Angebote zu Apple, Samsung, Fritz und Co. in der Übersicht
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Der Black Friday findet in den USA traditionell nach dem Thanksgiving-Feiertag statt. Ursprünglich nutzen Familien das lange, freie Wochenende, um am Freitag nach dem Festessen Weihnachtsgeschenke einzukaufen. Mittlerweile findet der Black Friday vor allem online statt und beschränkt sich längst nicht mehr nur auf diesen einen Tag. Seit Wochen werben Händler mit Deals, Schnäppchen und Angeboten. Doch nicht bei jedem beworbenen Produkt handelt es sich auch um ein gutes Angebot. Oft rechnen die Händler die vermeintliche Ersparnis einfach von der ursprünglichen Preisempfehlung der Hersteller herunter. Oft sieht der reale Preis längst anders aus. Entsprechend schwer ist es, wirklich gute Deals zu identifizieren. Wir haben uns deswegen für euch durch die Angebote geklickt.
Apple: iPhone, iPad, Mac Mini
Gute iPhone-Deals zum Black Friday sind selten. Einer, der zumindest nicht verkehrt ist, ist jener von Mediamarkt und Saturn zum iPhone Air. Das bei den Fans durchgefallene Gerät gibt es bei den Elektronikfachhändlern für 799 Euro. Wer zugreifen will, sollte sich vorab darüber im Klaren sein, dass viele Tester die mittelmäßige Akkulaufzeit kritisierten und das iPhone nur eine Kamera hat. articles.title: Los los cocineros y nutricionistas coinciden: "El salmón será más saludable y jugoso si lo cocinas con zumo de naranja en vez de con aceite."
articles.text:
Si tienes un par de lomos de salmón en la nevera y te apetece algo diferente de la plancha de siempre, puedes probar de una receta de salmón a la naranja y tirar de esta fruta para preparar una salsa en la que el pescado termina de cocinarse. Además, tanto los cocineros como los nutricionistas coinciden en que con este zumo el resultado será más jugoso y saludable que con aceite.
Características del salmón. El salmón un pescado graso con las propiedades típicas de los pescados azules: 12 gramos de lípidos por cada 100 gramos de porción comestible, una cantidad parecida a la de los atunes o los reos, y aportes importantes de ácidos grasos monoinsaturados y poliinsaturados, entre ellos omega 3 y omega 6. Además, también es una rica fuente de proteínas.
Lo que vas a necesitar. Para la receta hacen falta dos lomos de salmón, 200 mililitros de zumo de naranja y un par de rodajas de la misma fruta, a los que se suman una cucharada de salsa de soja, otra de miel, una cucharadita de jengibre rallado, un diente de ajo, una cucharada de aceite, sal y pimienta. Al final también se utiliza cebollino para decorar, aunque no aparece en la lista de ingredientes.
Primero, la salsa. Pero antes de encender el fuego toca preparar la salsa: se ralla la piel de la naranja, se exprime para sacar el zumo y se ralla también el jengibre, y después se mezcla todo con la miel y la soja hasta que quede homogéneo. Por último, se pica el diente de ajo y se añade a la mezcla.
El salmón, en dos tiempos. Con la salsa lista, el salmón va a una sartén con un poco de aceite de oliva y se cocina levemente, con cuidado de que no se quede seco. No pasa nada si parece algo crudo, ya que después vuelve al fuego. Y es que, una vez retirado el salmón y reservado en un plato, en esa misma sartén se vierte la salsa y se cocina a fuego medio hasta que reduce, se deja unos minutos para que espese y se incorpora de nuevo el pescado para que se cocine un poco más y coja todos los sabores.
Para servirlo, se colocan los lomos en una fuente, se bañan con la salsa para que se impregnen bien y se coronan con unas rodajas de naranja fresca y algo de cebollino al gusto.
Foto | Caroline Attwood
En Directo al Paladar | Esta es la receta saludable que hago cuando quiero un dulce: sin harina, sin mantequilla, sin azúcar añadido y sin horno

articles.title: In Other News: Tanker Cyberattacks, EU Quantum Act, New VirusTotal Capabilities
articles.text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.
Here are this week’s highlights:
ChatGPT Sites exposure
Pluto researchers combed web archives, public code repositories, search engines and other sources and found 16,666 sites created with ChatGPT Sites (which builds and hosts web apps for ChatGPT and Codex users), 12,830 of which were accessible to anyone. Manual checks confirmed sensitive data exposure at 27 organizations, including a Fortune 500 company’s sales dashboard, a freight forwarder’s customer quotes, and a vendor’s sales pitch. Sites are visible only to their owners and admins unless shared, but owners can open them to the entire internet.
RansomwareHelp co-founder accused of profiting from ransom payments
US authorities have charged Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, a Colombian national and co-founder of the ransomware recovery firm RansomwareHelp, with three counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors allege that instead of using its own decryption technology as advertised, his company purchased decryptors from cybercriminals at prices significantly lower than what it charged customers. In one case involving undercover FBI agents, Palacio allegedly paid a $6,000 ransom and billed the purported victim $13,260 for decrypting their files.
USDA payment systems breach
A system used by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make payments to farmers has been breached, according to NBC News. Two former department officials said the intrusion could let hackers access databases containing sensitive information on food safety and diseases carried by animals.
SolarWinds and Adobe patch vulnerabilities
SolarWinds has patched several critical vulnerabilities in its Serv-U managed file transfer product, including flaws that can lead to privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution. Adobe has addressed critical security holes in Campaign Classic and Experience Manager, including ones that allow arbitrary code execution, and a medium-severity DoS vulnerability in InDesign.
Container Store restores systems after cyberattack
US retailer The Container Store has restored its systems following a cyberattack that prevented customers from placing orders online. There is currently no evidence that customers’ financial information was stolen. The n0n ransomware group listed the company on its leak site earlier this month, but The Container Store has not addressed the claim.
VirusTotal adds new ransomware detection capabilities
VirusTotal has introduced new ransomware detection capabilities that rely on evidence of user files being encrypted during sandbox analysis. The improvements include a new behavior tag and stricter requirements for assigning the MITRE ATT&CK technique associated with data encryption for impact. VirusTotal demonstrated the effectiveness of the changes against ransomware that evaded detection by all 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis.
$17 billion targeted in US government anti-scam operation
The US Justice Department’s crackdown on fraud has targeted more than 800 defendants across over 400 cases since March. Authorities have also helped disrupt scam centers in more than 10 countries. According to the FBI, its Operation Blackout has led to the seizure or restraint of nearly $17 billion.
McDonald’s Japan hacked
McDonald’s Japan has disclosed a breach involving a database storing information associated with its mobile application. Hackers gained access to customer purchase histories, device location information, internal customer identifiers and IP addresses, but not names, contact details or credit card data. The number of impacted customers has not been disclosed.
Bithumb uncovers wider breach
South Korean cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb says more individuals and more types of personal information were compromised in an October cyberattack than initially reported. Bithumb also said the hackers had access for more than two weeks, not one hour as initially believed. The hackers stole data from an internal collaboration system, including identity documents, bank account numbers, transaction histories, and crypto wallet addresses. South Korean media reported that the initial victim count exceeded 7,000, including customers and staff.
Artex gains traction among state-sponsored hackers
Microsoft has observed several state-sponsored hacking groups, including China’s Salt Typhoon, as well as cybercriminals using the AI-powered penetration testing framework Artex. Hackers have leveraged the tool to identify exposed secrets in public code repositories, conduct supply chain attacks and find vulnerable systems. Microsoft says the framework can significantly accelerate intrusions, with attackers achieving privileged access and establishing persistence within minutes.
Quantum Act targets Europe’s cryptographic readiness
The European Commission’s proposed Quantum Act includes measures to accelerate the development and adoption of post-quantum cryptography and prepare the EU for the security risks posed by quantum computers. The legislation is part of a broader effort to strengthen Europe’s quantum technology industry, reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and establish global leadership in the field by 2030.
Tanker cyberattacks
Up to 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially dangerous cargo are believed to have been targeted in a wave of cyberattacks, according to The Wall Street Journal. US authorities are investigating whether Iran is responsible for the attacks.
Radware hacked
An internal report obtained by BleepingComputer shows that hackers breached cybersecurity firm Radware through an unprotected Cloud WAF management API exposed to the internet. Customer contact information and credentials associated with AWS, Azure and SFTP storage used by some customers may have been compromised. The company has not responded to SecurityWeek’s request for comment.
Related: In Other News: New CISA Director Nominee, Connected Car Hacking, Baker Tilly Data Breach

articles.title: A year from now, VMware wants AI troubleshooting your private cloud
articles.text:
A year from now, VMware wants AI troubleshooting your private cloud
A developer who needs two containers to test a change or modification has a different problem from a platform engineer running an application across several Kubernetes clusters.
Both need infrastructure, preferably before the ticket asking for it becomes old enough to have a birthday. Broadcom’s pitch for VMware Cloud Foundation is that the same private cloud can serve both teams, along with the people who still need virtual machines.
In an interview recorded recently at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon 2026 in Salt Lake City, The New Stack’s Nick Lucchesi asked Mark Chuang, senior director of product marketing for VMware Cloud Foundation at Broadcom, what developers and operators notice when they mix a cocktail of VMs, containers, and AI workloads onto one platform.
“They get a public cloud-like experience when it comes to self-service.”
“They get a public cloud-like experience when it comes to self-service,” Chuang told TNS, starting with the experience of asking for resources. “Platform teams still set the policies that govern those resources.”
This indeed matters when an AI application depends on services running in both containers and VMs. Operators can apply common security policies, manage the lifecycle of those workloads, and decide where they run. Developers can use self-service to get the infrastructure they need and continue working with their existing CI/CD tools, Chuang said.
How much orchestration do you need?
Chuang describes direct container deployment as an option for lightweight edge applications or quick developer checks. Kubernetes makes sense when an application needs automated orchestration across clusters. For a team testing a small change, spinning up a couple of containers directly can save setup work. For a platform team, both approaches fit into the same operating environment.
Lucchesi also asks what Broadcom means when it says a partner application has been validated for vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS). Chuang explains that Broadcom provides test environments and automated tools, while the software vendors define the tests appropriate to their applications.
“We’re just trying to lighten some of the load that’s on the plate of our customers.”
The checks can cover initial deployment, recovery from failure, security, and even a clean uninstall. Broadcom reviews the results, and partners use them to produce reference architectures and technical guidance.
“We’re just trying to lighten some of the load that’s on the plate of our customers,” Chuang said.
What if an update breaks a partner application anyway? Chuang says customers can contact either Broadcom or the software vendor. If they call Broadcom, its support team starts by trying to determine whether the problem came from the platform or the application update. That’s a practical detail for a developer who knows exactly when something stopped working and has several plausible explanations.
The tools teams already reach for
Broadcom also packages frequently used tools such as Prometheus, Argo CD and Harbor as VKS add-ons. Chuang says the company looks at usage and customer feedback when deciding what to include. Handling installation and updates through VKS takes work off teams that would otherwise have to maintain those integrations themselves.
The conversation touches on a change Chuang has noticed among customers. Some are increasingly willing to accept a curated set of tools if it gets them to a working environment faster.
“Is it a storage issue? Is it a network issue? Is it a CPU contention issue?”
TNS also asked Chuang which job a private cloud might take off an operator’s hands a year from now. Chuang’s answer starts with a familiar complaint about a slow application.
“Is it a storage issue? Is it a network issue? Is it a CPU contention issue?” Chuang asked, rhetorically. A year from now, Chuang expects AI to do more of the diagnostic work across those layers.
Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel for his take on what that could look like, what partner validation actually buys a developer, and why the quickest path to testing a container sometimes starts with a smaller deployment.

articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
  November 13, 2026
- Source:
  Princeton University
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Princeton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- John Mark P. Martirez. A Chemist’sGuide to Solid-State Qubits: DiamondColor Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules. ACS Central Science, 2026; 12 (10): 1578 DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548

articles.title: Sony’s 1000XM4C headphones are a Black Friday bargain at $198
articles.text:
Instead of purely looking forward with its headphone designs, Sony went back to its popular WH-1000XM4 design and made some improvements to make it even better. The 2026 version, called the WH-1000XM4C, sounds nearly as good as the pricier XM6 model (currently $348), but is down to $198 during Black Friday at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart. That’s $100 off their October launch price.
Sony’s 1000XM4C headphones are a Black Friday bargain at $198
All three colors (including the stunning lavender) are down to their lowest price yet just a few months after launch.
There’s a reason why Sony went back to refine the XM4. Our former reviewer Chris Welch praised them for being super comfortable and for having close to perfect features for the price, especially compared to its successor, the XM3 (still my daily driver, for what it’s worth). The XM4s had better sound quality and noise cancellation, plus improved mics, multipoint connectivity, and a sensor that can detect when you remove them to automatically pause audio. Now, with the XM4C, there are further improvements, most notably a 10-band equalizer in the app (compared to the original XM4’s five-band) that my colleague John Higgins says really helped the headphones’ midrange frequencies open up.
These are a great buy, but they aren’t your only Sony headphones deal to consider right now. Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are available during Black Friday at Best Buy for $169, their lowest price yet from a major retailer. There are upsides and downsides to this model: They feature improved noise cancellation thanks to more mics, despite using the same ANC chip as the XM4C, but they can’t fold up as compactly, making them a little bigger to pack in your bag. Either one you choose, you’ll have some great headphones to listen to going into 2027.

articles.title: Microsoft pushes emergency hotpatch to fix Windows Server crashes
articles.text:
Microsoft has released an emergency hotpatch update to address Windows Server 2025 crashes triggered after installing this month's security hotpatch update (KB5131077).
According to Microsoft, the KB5138318 out-of-band update should address stop errors with 0x139 codes triggered on affected servers when IPv6 routes expire.
"Microsoft has released a new Windows out-of-band (OOB) update today, November 25, 2026, to address an issue affecting a limited number of Windows Servers with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes," it said in a message center update.
"Affected devices might stop unexpectedly with stop error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE) when a route timer expires. This issue affects some Windows Server 2025 devices after installing the November 2026 Windows security hotpatch update."
This emergency non-security update is now rolling out to affected Windows Server 2025 devices enrolled in hotpatch updates through Windows Update.
KB5138318 will download and install automatically and will take effect without requiring IT administrators or users to restart affected devices.
The November 2026 hotpatch updates are also causing issues for Windows 11 users, who are experiencing installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications, as well as printing issues on systems running Forcepoint's DLP Endpoint Agent data loss prevention solution after installing this month's hotpatch on Windows 11 systems.
Windows Autopatch reached public preview in early June after an initial unveil in April 2022 and has been generally available since July 2022.
Microsoft announced earlier this year, in March, that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Microsoft Intune, after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed.
One month later, Microsoft fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that was causing driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices in the European Union.

articles.title: La Renault 5 reste sur le podium des ventes électriques européennes en octobre alors que la Twingo s’invite à la fête
articles.text:
Même si elle n’est plus une véritable nouveauté, la Renault 5 continue à bénéficier d’une excellente dynamique commerciale. Le Losange s’en réjouira, d’autant plus que la performance n’est pas uniquement cloisonnée à la France, en s’étendant à toute l’Europe. Une première place aurait été belle, mais elle reste occupée par le très solide Skoda Elroq. Le Tchèque s’est en effet vendu à 9 384 exemplaires au mois d’octobre.
Si la baisse de 17,6 % sur un an est la plus forte de ce classement, elle ne peut l’empêcher de garder sa couronne. La Renault 5, donc, arrive derrière, avec 8 933 unités écoulées, soit une diminution de 4,5 %. Malgré son grand âge, le BMW iX1 parvient à clore le podium avec 8 359 modèles vendus. Il doit ses beaux résultats à une politique tarifaire particulièrement agressive avec des loyers très attractifs.
Le Tesla Model Y bondit de plus de 50 %, les SUV allemands en embuscade
C’est d’ailleurs l’Allemand qui étonne le plus, lui qui n’était pas arrivé aussi haut depuis bien longtemps avec une progression de 36,8 % de ses ventes. En quatrième position, le Tesla Model Y demeure solide sur ses appuis avec 8 309 unités écoulées. L’Américain enregistre même la plus forte hausse des ventes avec +51,2 %. Juste derrière arrive une nouveauté, le Mercedes GLC, qui s’est habilement frayé un chemin avec 7 858 exemplaires.
Le Skoda Enyaq opère pour sa part une jolie remontée avec 7 561 modèles pour une hausse de ses ventes de 23,5 %. De quoi lui permettre de décrocher la sixième position du classement. Le Volkswagen ID.4, qui n’est autre que son cousin technique, le suit de très près avec 7 546 unités écoulées représentant une petite augmentation de 8,2 % de ses ventes. Il faut dire que négocier les prix s’avère désormais très facile depuis l’arrivée de l’ID. Tiguan en concession.
La Renault Twingo crée la surprise dans le top 10, aucune chinoise à l’horizon
Très facile et prévisible est aussi l’entrée de l’excellent BMW iX3 dans le top 10 des ventes. Le SUV bavarois signe ainsi une huitième place méritée avec ses 7 394 exemplaires. Le style Neue Klasse enrobant une fiche technique pointue semble avoir fait mouche auprès des clients. Seule berline du classement, la Volkswagen ID.7 fait figure d’outsider avec 7 011 unités pour une timide hausse de ses ventes de 0,7 %.
Enfin, l’auto s’invitant à la dixième place n’a rien d’anecdotique puisqu’il s’agit de notre bien aimée Renault Twingo. Avec 6 870 ventes, la grenouille montre d’ores et déjà son potentiel à l’échelle européenne. Au point de grappiller des places pour rejoindre la R5 ? Nous n’en sommes pas certains, cette dernière ayant récemment gagné en compétitivité avec une autonomie augmentée. Nous aurons confirmation avec les chiffres de fin d’année.

articles.title: Le clavier Logitech G Pro X Rapid passe à 189,99 € pour le Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le clavier Logitech G Pro X Rapid à 189,99 € (-16%)
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le clavier Logitech G Pro X Rapid passe à 189,99 € chez Amazon et Boulanger.com, soit une baisse d'environ 16 % et 37,19 € d'économie. Doté d'une frappe agréable grâce à ses commutateurs magnétiques personnalisables, ce modèle filaire affiche une note actuelle de 4/5 dans nos tests.
Logitech propose avec le G Pro X Rapid un clavier pour le jeu au format TKL (sans pavé numérique), conçu pour l'esport grâce à des interrupteurs analogiques à effet Hall. Ce modèle pensé pour la compétition s'est distingué lors de son passage dans notre labo grâce à sa frappe agréable et sa fabrication soignée.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, ce clavier descend à 189,99 € chez Amazon et Boulanger.com, soit environ 16 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (227,18 €). Cette baisse de prix permet d'économiser 37,19 €.
Des touches magnétiques personnalisables et un écran Oled intégré
Sur le bureau, ce modèle se concentre sur les performances en jeu compétitif grâce à ses interrupteurs magnétiques, qui permettent d'ajuster les points d'actionnement selon votre style de frappe. Le clavier intègre également la fonction SOCD-Cleaner pour optimiser la réactivité des commandes lors des déplacements rapides. Comme le souligne notre test complet, la présence d'un écran Oled apporte un vrai confort pour vérifier ses réglages à la volée.
Logitech G Pro X Rapid
Points forts

- Switches magnétiques personnalisables.
- Écran Oled pratique.
- Son et frappe agréables.
Points faibles

Une utilisation uniquement filaire et des finitions à parfaire
Actuellement noté 4/5, le clavier impose néanmoins quelques limites pratiques avec sa connectivité filaire exclusive, qui décevra les joueurs cherchant à épurer leur installation sans câble. Le repose-poignets adopte par ailleurs une forme étrange et la sérigraphie reste perfectible. Le Pro X TKL Rapid propose lui aussi des commutateurs analogiques couplés au logiciel de la marque pour ajuster finement chaque commande. Les deux modèles partagent d'ailleurs la même note actuelle de 4/5 dans nos tests, ainsi qu'une liaison filaire sans possibilité de connexion sans fil.
Le Logitech Pro X TKL Rapid coûte 84,55 € de moins que le Logitech G Pro X Rapid remisé, mais il fait l'impasse sur l'écran Oled et le repose-poignets.
